title: Defensive Shape Foundations
primarySkill: Establishing a connected defensive shape behind the ball.
objective: Develop players’ ability to form, maintain and adjust a compact defensive shape as the football moves across the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a rectangular playing area with a target gate at each end.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Begin with the attacking team holding possession at one end.
Position the defenders between the football and the opposite target gate.
The attacking team moves the football by kick or handball but initially does not attempt to score.
Defenders are restricted to shadow pressure during the first phase.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team circulates the football across and through the area.
Defenders move as a connected unit, maintaining appropriate width, depth and spacing.
When the football moves laterally, the defensive group slides together rather than chasing individually.
The nearest defender applies controlled pressure while teammates protect central and deeper space.
The coach occasionally calls “freeze” and checks the location, spacing and body position of each defender.
After five successful attacking possessions, the attacking team attempts to move the football through the target gate.
Defenders score one point for forcing the attack backwards, wide or into a turnover.
Teams rotate roles after two minutes.
coachingPoints: Maintain a compact shape between the football and the scoring target.
Move when the football moves rather than reacting after the receiver has taken possession.
The nearest defender presses while the next defenders provide cover.
Protect the corridor and force the attack towards wider, less dangerous areas.
Maintain enough spacing to cover ground without creating large gaps.
Communicate the location of opponents, space and possible switches.
Defenders behind the play must scan both the football and their direct opponent.
Reset the shape immediately after every disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders move together or as disconnected individuals.
Whether the nearest defender applies pressure without opening central space.
Whether deeper defenders remain goal-side.
Whether players communicate before the football arrives.
Whether the defensive line becomes too flat or too stretched.
How quickly the group resets after the football changes direction.
progressions: Allow attackers to score immediately through either target gate.
Add an attacking player who begins behind the defensive line.
Introduce live intercepts and controlled tackling.
Award double points for an attacking score through the corridor.
Begin each repetition from a turnover so defenders must recover into shape.
regressions: Use handball only to slow the movement of the football.
Mark defensive reference zones with cones.
Allow the coach to stop play frequently and physically reposition players.
successIndicators: Maintain connected spacing as the football moves.
Protect the corridor before pressuring wide possession.
Identify the pressure, cover and deeper-defender roles.
Reset their shape within two to three seconds of each disposal.
matchApplication: This drill introduces the basic team-defence shape required when the opposition controls possession. It teaches defenders to protect dangerous central space, support the player applying pressure and prevent one disposal from breaking the entire defensive structure.

title: Goal-Side Positioning Fundamentals
primarySkill: Maintaining goal-side positioning against an opponent.
objective: Teach defenders to remain between their opponent and the scoring target while still applying effective pressure to the football.
equipment: 1 scoring gate or pair of portable goals
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with a scoring gate at one end.
Pair each attacker with a defender.
Position attackers between 15 and 25 metres from the scoring gate.
Begin with a feeder holding the football outside the area.
Defenders start one to two metres from their opponent in a goal-side position.
The first phase is non-contact apart from controlled body positioning.
howTheDrillWorks:
Attackers move within the area attempting to create separation from their defender.
Defenders track their opponent while staying between the opponent and the scoring gate.
The feeder selects an attacker and delivers the football by kick or handball.
The defender attempts to spoil, intercept or force the attacker away from the scoring gate.
If the attacker gains possession, they have five seconds to score through the gate.
Defenders score one point for maintaining goal-side position and forcing the attacker away from goal.
They score two points for an intercept or clean spoil.
Rotate the feeder and swap attacking and defensive roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Begin in a position that protects the scoring side of the opponent.
Keep the hips and shoulders open enough to see both the football and the opponent.
Adjust the distance from the opponent according to the position of the football.
Close space as the feeder prepares to dispose of the football.
Avoid standing directly behind the opponent where movement cannot be seen.
Use small adjustment steps rather than crossing the feet.
Recover goal-side immediately if the opponent gains separation.
Communicate when another defender may need to switch or assist.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders begin between their opponent and the scoring target.
Whether defenders can see both the opponent and the football.
Whether defenders close space at the correct time.
Whether players lose balance by crossing their feet.
Whether beaten defenders recover through the inside rather than chasing from behind.
Whether defenders force attackers towards less dangerous space.
progressions: Allow attackers to lead in any direction before turning towards goal.
Add a second attacker and defender to create potential switches.
Permit full live contests and legal tackling.
Use a kick rather than a handball from the feeder.
Introduce a second scoring gate to increase scanning demands.
regressions: Restrict attackers to one nominated leading direction.
Reduce the size of the area.
Allow defenders to begin closer to their opponent.
successIndicators: Remain between their opponent and the scoring target.
See both the football and their direct opponent.
Close space as the disposal is prepared.
Force possession away from the central scoring line.
Recover goal-side quickly when initially beaten.
matchApplication: Goal-side positioning is essential when defending leading forwards, midfielders pushing inside 50 and opponents spreading from stoppages. The drill teaches defenders to protect the most dangerous route to goal before attempting to win possession.

title: Corridor Protection Gate
primarySkill: Protecting the corridor and forcing opposition possession wide.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to deny central ball movement and guide the opposition towards wider, less dangerous areas.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 40 metres wide, with a central corridor 12 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular playing area.
Use cones to create a 12-metre-wide corridor through the centre.
Place one scoring gate at the end of the corridor and two wider scoring gates near the boundaries.
Divide players into attackers and defenders.
The attacking team starts with possession at one end.
Defenders begin in a compact shape protecting the central gate.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move the football through any scoring gate.
A score through the central gate is worth three points.
A score through a wide gate is worth one point.
The defending team applies angled pressure designed to close the corridor and guide possession wide.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier while teammates close central passing lanes.
Defenders score two points for an intercept and one point for forcing a turnover outside the corridor.
After a turnover, the defending team has five seconds to move the football back through the starting line.
Teams swap roles after three minutes.
coachingPoints: Protect the central gate before applying pressure to wide possession.
Approach the ball carrier on an angle that removes the inside option.
The second defender must protect the next central receiver.
Keep the deepest defender aligned with the corridor.
Do not overcollapse towards the football and leave the opposite side completely open.
Communicate when the football is likely to switch.
Adjust the team shape early as the ball carrier prepares to dispose of the football.
Force high, slow or difficult kicks towards the boundary.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether pressure is applied from the correct angle.
Whether the corridor is protected by more than one defensive layer.
Whether defenders become attracted to wide possession unnecessarily.
Whether the deepest defender remains centrally positioned.
Whether the weak-side defenders scan and adjust.
Whether turnovers are created in predictable wide areas.
progressions: Reduce the width of the defensive corridor.
Allow attackers to run and carry before disposing.
Introduce full tackling.
Award attackers five points for a corridor score.
Start the drill from different field positions, including half-back and the wing.
regressions: Increase the width of the corridor.
Allow the defence to begin set before each repetition.
successIndicators: Apply pressure from an inside-out angle.
Maintain cover behind the pressing defender.
Force the opposition to use wider, slower routes.
Create turnovers near the boundary or outside the corridor.
matchApplication: The drill replicates defending opposition ball movement from defensive 50, through the centre square or into attacking 50. It teaches the team to remove the shortest path to goal and force possession into less dangerous areas.

title: Defensive Line Connection
primarySkill: Maintaining effective spacing and connection between defensive lines.
objective: Develop the ability of defenders, midfielders and high forwards to move as connected lines without allowing exploitable space between them.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground, approximately 90 metres long × 60 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the defensive team into three connected lines: high defenders, midfield defenders and deep defenders.
Space the lines approximately 15–20 metres apart.
Position an attacking team across the same area.
The attack begins with the football at one end.
Mark two horizontal reference lines to help players recognise excessive spacing.
Nominate one player in each line as the primary communicator.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football through the area using kicks and handballs.
The defensive lines slide forwards, backwards and laterally according to the position of the football.
The objective is to prevent the attack from receiving uncontested possession between the defensive lines.
If the football moves backwards, the defence steps forward together.
If the attack breaks a line, the next defensive line delays the ball carrier while the beaten line recovers.
The coach calls “freeze” at selected moments to measure spacing and identify gaps.
The defence scores one point for forcing a backwards disposal and two points for an intercept.
On a turnover, the defenders attempt to exit through a wide target gate.
coachingPoints: Maintain approximately 15–20 metres between lines, adjusting for the speed and position of the football.
Move as the ball carrier prepares to dispose, not after the next player receives.
The line nearest the football applies pressure while the next line provides depth and cover.
Avoid having all three lines become flat.
Communicators must organise players who cannot see the entire shape.
Step forward when the opposition retreats.
Drop together when the opposition has time and space to kick over the line.
Recover behind the football immediately after a line is broken.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
The distance between each defensive line.
Whether players step and drop together.
Whether gaps appear between midfield and deep defenders.
Whether the deepest players provide early instructions.
Whether the front line continues to defend after being bypassed.
Whether the team becomes compressed too close to the football.
progressions: Remove the reference lines.
Increase the playing length.
Add live tackling and contested marking.
Award attackers bonus points for receiving between lines.
Begin from a rapid turnover so the defence must organise while moving.
successIndicators: Step forward when the opposition retreats.
Prevent uncontested possession between defensive layers.
Recover quickly after a line is broken.
Use communication to adjust players behind the football.
matchApplication: Connected defensive lines prevent opposition players from finding uncontested space between the midfield and defensive 50. The drill develops the coordinated movement required to compress the ground, defend repeated possessions and protect the space behind the ball.

title: Man-on-Man Accountability Grid
primarySkill: Maintaining direct defensive accountability for an opponent.
objective: Teach players to remain accountable for a direct opponent while responding appropriately to movement, switches and changes in possession.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a square playing area with a scoring gate at each end.
Pair every attacker with a defender.
Use numbered or matched bibs to make each pairing clear.
The attacking team begins with possession.
Defenders must initially remain responsible for their nominated opponent.
Controlled body contact is permitted, but tackling can be delayed until the progression.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football through the grid and attempts to score through the opposite gate.
Each defender tracks their nominated opponent and protects the scoring side.
If two attackers cross paths, defenders may switch opponents only after clear communication.
A defender who leaves their opponent to pressure the football must have a teammate covering the released player.
The defending team scores one point for forcing an ineffective disposal and two points for an intercept.
If an attacker receives uncontested possession more than five metres from their defender, the attack receives a bonus point.
Following a turnover, teams immediately change direction.
Rotate pairings every three minutes.
coachingPoints: Know the location of the direct opponent before looking for the football.
Maintain goal-side position whenever the attack is moving towards goal.
Use an open stance to see both the football and the opponent.
Communicate before switching opponents.
Do not leave an opponent unless pressure on the ball is necessary and cover is available.
Use legal body positioning to deny leading lanes.
Recover quickly if an opponent gains separation.
Re-establish match-ups immediately after a turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether each defender knows their direct opponent.
Whether defenders remain goal-side.
Whether switches are communicated early.
Whether players leave opponents unnecessarily.
Whether defenders use legal body positioning.
Whether accountability is re-established after turnovers.
progressions: Introduce full legal tackling.
Remove numbered bibs.
Add a neutral attacking player to create temporary overloads.
Require defenders to decide when to switch from man-on-man to space protection.
Increase the size of the grid.
regressions: Stop play after every switch to confirm responsibilities.
successIndicators: Identify and track a direct opponent.
Communicate and complete switches without leaving free players.
Apply pressure without abandoning defensive responsibility.
matchApplication: Man-on-man accountability is used at stoppages, kick-ins, late-game scenarios and against teams with dangerous individual players. The drill teaches defenders to balance direct responsibility with the need to support teammates.

title: Intercept Shape and Launch
primarySkill: Creating an intercepting position behind pressure on the football.
objective: Develop the defensive shape and anticipation required to intercept opposition disposals and immediately launch an attacking transition.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with one attacking target gate and two wide defensive exit gates.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
Position one defender as the pressure player, two as cover defenders and one as the deepest interceptor.
Place attackers across multiple lanes.
Begin each repetition with an attacker in possession near one end.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move the football through the central target gate.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier and attempts to influence the direction and height of the disposal.
Cover defenders close short options and protect the corridor.
The deepest defender positions where they can read and attack the likely kick.
If the defence intercepts, the intercepting player immediately selects one of the two wide exit gates.
Teammates spread to provide an exit option while one player protects behind the football.
The defence scores two points for an intercept and an additional point for exiting successfully.
Rotate pressure, cover and intercept roles after each block.
coachingPoints: Pressure on the ball must influence where the disposal can go.
The interceptor should position off the opponent rather than directly beside them.
Read the ball carrier’s body position, eyes and preferred kicking side.
Maintain enough depth to move forward towards the football.
Cover defenders must protect short and central options.
Communicate when an intercepting player is leaving an opponent.
After the intercept, spread quickly and use the safest effective exit.
Retain one player behind the football during the rebound.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether pressure influences the attacking disposal.
Whether the interceptor reads the play before the football is kicked.
Whether the interceptor begins with suitable depth.
Whether cover defenders protect the space underneath.
Whether teammates spread immediately after the turnover.
Whether the first exit disposal is safe and purposeful.
progressions: Add a second possible interceptor.
Introduce full contested marking and tackling.
Allow attackers to switch the football before entering.
Award extra points for an intercept that leads to a score.
Begin from different field positions.
regressions: Use predictable kicks from a coach.
Reduce the number of attacking options.
Mark the preferred intercept area with cones.
successIndicators: Position with suitable depth to intercept.
Read and attack the football early.
Launch a controlled exit immediately after winning possession.
matchApplication: Intercept defence is central to modern Australian football. The drill develops the relationship between pressure on the ball, cover underneath and a defender positioned to win the next kick before transitioning rapidly into attack.

title: Ball-Side Pressure and Weak-Side Cover
primarySkill: Coordinating pressure near the football with cover away from the football.
objective: Develop coordinated defensive movement in which ball-side players pressure possession while weak-side players protect central space and prepare for a switch.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into a ball-side half and a weak-side half using a line of cones.
Place two target gates at each end.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
The attacking team begins with possession on one side.
Defenders match the attackers but are encouraged to defend space rather than remain directly beside opponents.
Begin with one neutral player supporting the attacking team.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move the football from one end to the other.
When the football is on one side, the nearest defenders apply pressure and close short options.
Weak-side defenders move towards central cover positions while maintaining awareness of opponents behind them.
The attacking team may switch the football across the area at any time.
On a switch, the weak-side defenders become the new pressure group while the original pressure group recovers into cover.
Defenders score two points for intercepting a switch and one point for forcing the attack backwards.
Attackers score through either target gate.
Teams rotate roles after three-minute blocks.
coachingPoints: Ball-side defenders must close space quickly without all attacking the same opponent.
Weak-side defenders protect the corridor before marking wide space.
Maintain vision of both the football and potential weak-side receivers.
Begin shifting before the football reaches the opposite side.
Communicate when a switch is likely.
The deepest defender should organise the weak-side cover.
Recover into central space after applying pressure.
Do not leave the far side completely unattended.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball-side pressure closes time and space.
Whether weak-side defenders become too wide or remain connected centrally.
Whether players recognise the preparation for a switch.
Whether the group changes roles quickly when the football changes sides.
Whether the deepest defender communicates effectively.
Whether defenders intercept or merely react to switches.
progressions: Remove the neutral player.
Add full tackling.
Award attackers extra points for a successful switch leading to a score.
Increase the width of the area.
Begin each repetition from an unpredictable turnover.
regressions: Restrict switches to a coach’s call.
Reduce the width of the area.
Allow the defence to begin set before the attack starts.
successIndicators: Apply immediate pressure around the football.
Recognise switches before the football travels.
Exchange pressure and cover roles smoothly.
matchApplication: The drill replicates defending teams that move the football from one side of the ground to the other. It teaches players away from the football to remain connected, protect the corridor and prepare to become the next pressure line.

title: Introductory Zone Defence
primarySkill: Defending allocated space within a basic zone structure.
objective: Introduce players to defending space, passing lanes and dangerous areas rather than following one opponent across the entire ground.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 45 metres wide, divided into six zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into six equal rectangular zones.
Position one or two defenders in each zone.
The attacking team may move freely through the entire area.
Defenders begin by remaining within their nominated zone.
Place a scoring gate at the end of the area.
The attack begins with possession at the opposite end.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move the football through the area and score.
Defenders protect passing lanes and dangerous space within their nominated zone.
When an attacker moves from one zone to another, the first defender communicates the handover.
The next defender assumes responsibility without both defenders following the same opponent.
Defenders may leave their zone temporarily to apply pressure if an adjacent teammate provides cover.
The defence scores one point for forcing a backwards disposal and two points for an intercept.
After a turnover, defenders attempt to exit through the starting line.
Rotate zone responsibilities after each block.
coachingPoints: Protect the most dangerous space within the zone rather than standing beside one opponent.
Maintain vision of the football, nearby opponents and adjacent defenders.
Communicate every handover.
Close space as the football enters the zone.
Avoid following an opponent so far that the zone is left open.
Slide as a connected unit when the football moves laterally.
Keep the deepest zone protected at all times.
Use body position to deny central passing lanes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders understand which space they are responsible for.
Whether handovers occur before an attacker becomes free.
Whether two defenders follow the same opponent.
Whether zones remain connected.
Whether central lanes are protected.
Whether pressure increases as the football enters a zone.
progressions: Remove visible zone boundaries.
Allow defenders greater freedom to press outside their zone.
Add full tackling.
Introduce a central neutral attacker.
Award attackers extra points for splitting two zones with one disposal.
regressions: Require attackers to pause briefly after receiving.
Allow the coach to direct defensive movement.
successIndicators: Protect dangerous passing lanes within their zone.
Apply pressure when possession enters their area.
Avoid being dragged away from central space.
matchApplication: Zone defence is used during opposition kick-ins, slow ball movement, forward-half pressure and protection of defensive 50. This drill introduces the principles of guarding space, handing over opponents and maintaining collective shape.

title: Press Trigger Recognition
primarySkill: Recognising and acting on cues to apply coordinated team pressure.
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise pressing triggers and apply coordinated pressure without breaking the defensive structure.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with a target gate at each end.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
Explain the approved press triggers:
A backwards handball
A slow or floating kick
A receiver facing their own goal
A poor ground ball
A player receiving near the boundary
A disposal to a stationary teammate
The attack begins with possession and attempts to score.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team circulates the football and attempts to move through the target gate.
The defence begins in a compact containment shape.
When a recognised trigger occurs, the nearest defender calls “press”.
All defenders respond by closing the ball carrier, nearby receivers and short exit options.
Weak-side and deeper defenders move forward to maintain connection behind the press.
If no trigger occurs, defenders remain patient and protect dangerous space.
Defenders score three points for a turnover created within five seconds of a press call.
Attackers score two points if they break the press and move through the target gate.
coachingPoints: Press only when the cue creates a genuine opportunity.
The nearest defender must communicate the trigger clearly.
The first defender pressures the ball carrier’s disposal.
Supporting defenders remove the closest safe options.
Deeper defenders step forward so the press remains connected.
Do not press individually without support.
If the press is broken, recover goal-side immediately.
Maintain legal, balanced closing technique.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players recognise the correct triggers.
Whether the press call is immediate and clear.
Whether all defenders respond together.
Whether the first defender closes under control.
Whether supporting players remove short options.
Whether deeper defenders step forward.
Whether the team recovers after the press is broken.
progressions: Remove the list of triggers and require players to identify opportunities independently.
Add full tackling.
Reduce the size of the area.
Add a neutral attacker to increase the difficulty of closing options.
Start repetitions from random loose-ball situations.
regressions: The coach calls each press trigger.
Increase the width of the area.
successIndicators: Apply coordinated pressure around the football.
Close the most likely escape options.
Recover quickly if the press is broken.
matchApplication: Pressing triggers appear when an opponent receives under pressure, faces their own goal, fumbles or is forced near the boundary. The drill teaches the team to convert those moments into coordinated pressure and turnovers.

title: Defensive Stop-to-Exit Decision
primarySkill: Selecting the correct first disposal after a defensive stop.
objective: Develop players’ ability to secure a defensive stop, scan immediately and choose an appropriate exit option based on pressure, space and teammate positioning.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use the defensive half of the ground.
Place one central exit gate and two wide exit gates near the centre line.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Begin with the attacking team entering towards goal.
Position defenders in a realistic defensive shape.
The coach starts each repetition with a kick, handball or loose football into the attacking area.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to score a goal.
The defending team must create a stop through a spoil, tackle, intercept or forced turnover.
Once possession is secured, the first player scans for three possible exits:
Immediate short release
Wide switch
Controlled central exit
Supporting defenders spread to create width and depth.
The defending team has eight seconds to move the football through one exit gate.
The central gate is worth three points but may only be used when it is clearly safe.
A wide exit is worth two points.
A rushed disposal that returns possession to the attacking team results in an immediate repeat entry.
Reset after a successful exit, score or second turnover.
coachingPoints: Secure the football before attempting the exit.
The first possession after a turnover must be composed and purposeful.
Scan before taking possession where possible.
Use a short release if a teammate is free and facing the ground.
Use width when the corridor is congested.
Take the central exit only when pressure has been removed.
Supporting players must spread immediately after the stop.
Retain defensive cover in case the exit fails.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players secure the football before disposing.
Whether the first receiver scans before possession.
Whether support players spread quickly.
Whether players choose an exit appropriate to the pressure.
Whether the central exit is used selectively.
Whether one defender remains behind the football.
How the team reacts when the first exit is blocked.
progressions: Reduce the exit time to six seconds.
Introduce full match-like contact.
Add a second attacking wave after the initial stop.
Require the defence to progress beyond the exit gate and complete a forward entry.
Alter the score and time scenario before each repetition.
regressions: Allow the defence one uncontested disposal after the turnover.
Begin from coach-directed intercepts rather than live entries.
successIndicators: Secure possession before attempting to rebound.
Scan and choose an exit suited to the pressure.
Exit the defensive area without conceding an immediate repeat entry.
matchApplication: The drill replicates the critical moment after a defensive turnover, when players must shift from stopping the opposition to retaining possession and exiting defensive 50. It teaches composure, support, risk management and the difference between safe and aggressive rebound options.

title: Pressure, Cover and Balance Rotation
primarySkill: Rotating between pressure, cover and balance roles as the football moves.
objective: Develop players’ ability to identify and exchange the three essential defensive roles of pressuring the ball carrier, covering the next option and balancing the space behind the contest.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular playing area with one target gate at each end.
Divide players into equal attacking and defending teams.
Begin with three defenders nominated as the pressure, cover and balance players.
Position the remaining defenders behind those three in connected support positions.
The attacking team begins with possession at one end.
Use controlled pressure during the introductory phase.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football by kick or handball towards the opposite target gate.
The nearest defender becomes the pressure player and closes the ball carrier.
The second defender protects the most dangerous short option and becomes the cover player.
The third defender positions behind and inside the first two defenders as the balance player.
When the football moves, defenders immediately rotate into the new pressure, cover and balance roles.
The coach may call “freeze” to ask each defender to identify their current role.
Defenders score one point for forcing play backwards and two points for an intercept.
Teams change roles after three-minute blocks.
coachingPoints: The nearest defender must apply pressure without running past the ball carrier.
The cover defender protects the next dangerous receiver rather than following the football.
The balance defender remains goal-side and protects space behind the first two defenders.
Players must exchange roles immediately when the football moves.
Pressure should guide the disposal towards the cover defender.
Defenders must communicate their role before the next disposal.
Avoid having two defenders perform the same role.
Recover into balance if the first pressure effort is broken.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the nearest defender recognises responsibility for pressure.
Whether the cover defender protects the most dangerous option.
Whether a balance defender remains behind the play.
Whether roles rotate as soon as possession changes.
Whether defenders communicate before the ball carrier disposes.
Whether the group retains structure after pressure is broken.
progressions: Allow full legal tackling.
Remove the nominated starting roles.
Add a neutral attacker to create temporary overloads.
Reduce the playing area.
Require an immediate defensive exit after a turnover.
regressions: Walk through each role before beginning live play.
Reduce the contest to three attackers against three defenders.
Allow the coach to call each defender’s role.
successIndicators: Identify pressure, cover and balance responsibilities.
Rotate roles immediately when the football moves.
Maintain a defender behind the first line of pressure.
Guide the attack towards defensive support.
Remain connected when the initial pressure is beaten.
matchApplication: The pressure, cover and balance relationship underpins team defence around every contest. It prevents defenders from chasing the same opponent, protects the next disposal and provides security if the ball carrier escapes the first pressure effort.

title: Delay and Recover Numbers
primarySkill: Delaying an opposition attack until defensive support recovers.
objective: Teach outnumbered defenders to slow the opposition, protect the most dangerous space and create time for teammates to recover behind the football.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with one central and two wide scoring gates at the attacking end.
Begin each repetition with three attackers against two defenders.
Position two recovering defenders 10–15 metres behind the starting attackers.
The coach begins play with a disposal to one attacker.
The central gate is worth more than the wide gates.
Rotate all players through attacking, initial defending and recovery roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
Three attackers move towards the scoring gates against two starting defenders.
The defenders retreat at a controlled angle while protecting the central gate.
The nearest defender applies enough pressure to slow the ball carrier without allowing an easy handball over the top.
The second defender protects the central receiver and communicates the location of support.
The two recovering defenders sprint back through the inside of the area.
Once the recovering defenders arrive, the defence may apply stronger pressure and attempt to force a turnover.
Attackers score three points through the central gate and one point through a wide gate.
Defenders score two points for delaying the attack until support arrives and three points for a turnover.
coachingPoints: Protect the central scoring route before attempting to win the football.
Retreat with controlled footwork rather than turning completely away from the attack.
Apply pressure that slows the ball carrier and influences the disposal.
Do not commit both starting defenders to the same opponent.
Recovering players must sprint through the shortest goal-side route.
Communicate when defensive numbers have been restored.
Once support arrives, transition from delay to active pressure.
Avoid conceding an uncontested disposal over the top.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders protect the central gate.
Whether the first defender slows the ball carrier.
Whether the second defender remains connected.
Whether recovering players use the shortest inside route.
Whether defenders recognise when numbers have been restored.
Whether pressure increases at the correct moment.
progressions: Begin with four attackers against two defenders.
Increase the recovery distance.
Add full tackling once support arrives.
Allow the attack to change direction and switch the football.
Add a second attacking wave after the first disposal.
regressions: Start recovering defenders closer to the contest.
successIndicators: Protect the central route while outnumbered.
Communicate when defensive numbers are restored.
matchApplication: Teams are frequently outnumbered immediately after a turnover. This drill teaches defenders to manage that disadvantage, deny the fastest route to goal and create enough time for teammates to recover into the defensive structure.

title: Boundary Trap Fundamentals
primarySkill: Using the boundary as an additional defensive barrier.
objective: Develop players’ ability to force opposition possession towards the boundary and close the remaining disposal options without allowing an easy release back into the corridor.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 25 metres wide, positioned beside a boundary line or marked sideline.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a narrow channel beside the boundary.
Place one attacking exit gate in the corridor-side corner and one gate further along the boundary.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
Begin with the attacking team in possession near the boundary.
Position one defender on the ball carrier and supporting defenders inside the play.
Explain that the boundary removes one direction from the attack.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to escape through either target gate.
The nearest defender approaches from the corridor side and forces the ball carrier towards the boundary.
Supporting defenders close short options along the line and prevent a handball back inside.
The deepest defender protects the kick over the top.
Defenders may tackle under controlled conditions.
The defence scores one point for forcing a boundary disposal and two points for a turnover.
The attack scores two points for escaping through the inside gate and one point through the boundary-side gate.
Teams rotate after three-minute blocks.
coachingPoints: Approach from inside to outside so the corridor is removed.
Avoid allowing the ball carrier to step back inside onto their preferred side.
The second defender closes the nearest release option.
The third defender protects the kick over the top.
Maintain legal pressure without forcing players dangerously across the boundary.
Communicate when the trap is established.
Do not overcommit so far forward that the attack can handball behind the pressure.
Reset inside the football if the opponent escapes backwards.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first defender closes from the corridor side.
Whether supporting defenders remove short escape options.
Whether a defender protects the space behind the trap.
Whether the attack is forced to dispose under pressure.
Whether defenders maintain safe legal contact.
Whether players reset if the trap is escaped.
progressions: Add full match-like tackling.
Allow the attack to switch backwards before attempting to escape.
Increase the length of the channel.
Begin from a loose football near the boundary.
Award the defence a bonus point for intercepting the inside release.
regressions: Allow the coach to nominate the attacking exit gate.
successIndicators: Protect the disposal over the pressure line.
Create stoppages, rushed disposals or turnovers in wide areas.
matchApplication: The boundary can function as an additional defender when pressure is applied from the correct angle. The drill develops the structure required to trap opposition possession near the line and prevent an easy return to central space.

title: Defending the Overlap Run
primarySkill: Defending a running overlap without losing control of the ball carrier.
objective: Teach defenders to recognise an overlap run, communicate responsibility and prevent the running receiver from breaking through the defensive line.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with a target gate at the attacking end.
Begin with two attackers against two defenders.
One attacker starts with the football while the second begins behind or beside the ball carrier.
Position the first defender on the ball carrier and the second defender goal-side of the supporting attacker.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
Begin at controlled speed before progressing to live play.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier moves forward while the second attacker accelerates on an overlap run.
The first defender pressures the ball carrier and attempts to delay the handball.
The second defender tracks the overlap runner while maintaining awareness of the ball carrier.
If the overlap runner receives, the defenders communicate and exchange pressure and cover roles.
The attackers attempt to score through the target gate.
Defenders score one point for preventing the overlap handball and two points for forcing a turnover.
If the overlap is completed, the nearest defender pressures the receiver while the other recovers inside.
Reset immediately and change the starting side.
coachingPoints: The first defender must pressure the ball carrier without turning their back on the overlap runner.
The second defender should track from a goal-side and inside position.
Communicate whether the defenders are staying with opponents or switching roles.
Delay the handball by closing the ball carrier’s preferred release side.
Avoid both defenders moving towards the overlap runner.
Recover through the inside if the handball breaks the line.
The covering defender must be prepared to become the next pressure player.
Maintain balanced footwork when changing direction.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball defender recognises the overlap.
Whether the second defender maintains goal-side position.
Whether responsibility is communicated before the handball.
Whether defenders exchange pressure and cover roles.
Whether the inside route remains protected.
Whether recovery begins immediately after the line is broken.
progressions: Add a third attacker who may lead in front of the ball.
Allow the ball carrier to kick instead of handballing.
Introduce full tackling.
Begin from a turnover with attackers already moving.
Add a second overlap runner from the opposite side.
regressions: Begin with the second defender closer to the runner.
successIndicators: Recognise the overlap before the receiver passes the ball carrier.
Delay or disrupt the release handball.
Recover into cover after the overlap is completed.
matchApplication: Overlap running is commonly used to break defensive lines through half-back, the wing and forward entry. This drill teaches defenders to manage the ball carrier and the running receiver without being drawn to the same opponent.

title: Crossing Leads Defensive Handover
primarySkill: Handing over opponents when attacking leads cross.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to communicate and exchange opponents when crossing leads make it inefficient or unsafe to remain with the original match-up.
equipment: 1 scoring gate or set of goals
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a forward-entry area with a feeder positioned 25–35 metres from goal.
Place two attackers and two defenders inside the area.
Attackers begin on opposite sides and prepare to make crossing leads.
Defenders begin goal-side and slightly inside their direct opponents.
Use additional pairs in separate grids where numbers allow.
Begin with predetermined leads before introducing choice.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the feeder’s movement, both attackers lead and cross through the centre of the area.
Defenders decide whether to remain with their original opponent or complete a handover.
A handover must include an early verbal call and clear visual confirmation.
The feeder delivers the football to either attacker.
Defenders attempt to spoil, intercept or force the receiver away from goal.
Attackers score by marking or receiving inside the scoring area.
Defenders score one point for a successful handover and two points for winning possession.
Rotate attackers, defenders and feeders after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Begin goal-side and protect the central leading lane.
Communicate before the attackers cross, not after separation occurs.
Use clear calls such as “switch”, “stay” and the teammate’s name.
Do not hand over an opponent unless the teammate is positioned to accept responsibility.
Maintain body contact legally through the crossing point.
After a handover, immediately locate the new opponent.
Protect the deeper and more dangerous lead.
Avoid both defenders following the same attacker.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders recognise the crossing pattern early.
Whether the handover call occurs before the attackers separate.
Whether both defenders understand the decision.
Whether the central lane remains protected.
Whether defenders locate the new opponent immediately.
Whether one attacker becomes free because of hesitation.
progressions: Allow attackers to fake the crossing lead.
Add a third attacker and defender.
Permit the feeder to delay or change the disposal.
Introduce full contested marking.
Begin from different forward-entry angles.
regressions: Mark the crossing point with a cone.
Reduce the size of the scoring area.
successIndicators: Communicate before the handover is required.
Remain goal-side of the new opponent.
Prevent attackers from gaining uncontested central possession.
matchApplication: Forwards regularly cross leads to create defensive confusion and separation. This drill develops the communication and positioning required to hand opponents over without allowing an uncontested mark in a dangerous scoring position.

title: Protecting the Top of Defensive 50
primarySkill: Protecting the central space at the top of defensive 50.
objective: Develop a connected defensive structure that denies central possession at the top of defensive 50 and forces opposition entries towards wider, lower-percentage areas.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line, using the full width of the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use the attacking half of the ground.
Mark a central protection zone approximately 25 metres wide at the top of defensive 50.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Position defenders in a connected line across the top of defensive 50 with deeper support behind them.
Begin each repetition with the attack controlling possession between the centre square and the 50-metre arc.
Place scoring markers in central and wide entry zones.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to enter inside 50 and create a scoring opportunity.
Defenders protect the central zone and apply inside-out pressure to the ball carrier.
The nearest defender closes the football while supporting defenders protect central leading lanes.
Deeper defenders position to intercept kicks directed towards goal.
Attackers score three points for a controlled central entry and one point for a wide entry.
Defenders score one point for forcing a wide entry and two points for an intercept or turnover.
After winning possession, defenders attempt to exit through a wide gate near the wing.
Reset after a score, successful exit or second turnover.
coachingPoints: Protect the central space at the top of defensive 50 before pressing wide possession.
Pressure the ball carrier from inside to outside.
Keep defenders connected across the width of the ground.
Midfield defenders must recover behind the football and close the space in front of key forwards.
Deep defenders should position with enough depth to attack the incoming kick.
Communicate leading forwards and players entering from behind.
Avoid all defenders collapsing below the football.
Prepare to spread immediately after an intercept.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the central protection zone remains occupied.
Whether pressure guides the entry towards the boundary.
Whether defenders track forwards entering central space.
Whether deep defenders hold suitable intercept depth.
Whether midfield defenders recover behind the football.
Whether the defensive group exits with width after a turnover.
progressions: Remove the marked central protection zone.
Add full match-like tackling and marking.
Allow the attack to switch across the full width.
Add a second attacking entry after an incomplete exit.
Introduce scoreboard and time scenarios.
regressions: Require the attack to begin from one side.
Allow the defence to set before each entry.
successIndicators: Position defenders to intercept rather than merely follow.
matchApplication: The top of defensive 50 is a high-value area because possession there allows direct entries to dangerous forwards. This drill teaches the team to protect that space, influence the entry direction and create intercept opportunities.

title: Repeat Entry Defensive Reset
primarySkill: Resetting defensive shape after an unsuccessful exit or repeat opposition entry.
objective: Develop players’ ability to recover, reorganise and defend a second opposition entry immediately after the first defensive exit breaks down.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use the defensive half of the ground.
Position attackers outside and inside defensive 50.
Arrange defenders in a realistic team shape.
Place two wide exit gates and one central exit gate near the centre line.
Keep spare footballs with coaches around the 50-metre arc.
Explain that a second football may be introduced after an incomplete defensive exit.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with an attacking entry inside 50.
The defence attempts to stop the attack and exit through a target gate.
If the exit is intercepted, goes out of bounds or misses the gate, the coach immediately introduces a second football.
Defenders must recover goal-side, identify new opponents and rebuild their shape.
Attackers immediately launch a repeat entry.
Defenders score one point for stopping the first entry, two points for stopping the repeat entry and three points for completing a successful exit.
Attackers score for any goal or controlled mark in a designated scoring zone.
Rotate positional groups after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: React immediately when the exit fails; do not stop to watch the turnover.
Recover through central goal-side positions before locating wide opponents.
The deepest defender must organise the reset.
Reassign opponents rather than attempting to find the original match-up.
Protect the top of defensive 50 and the corridor first.
Communicate whether players are pressing, covering or holding depth.
Maintain composure despite fatigue and repeated entries.
After the second stop, choose a safer exit if the first option failed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
The speed of the reaction after the failed exit.
Whether defenders recover centrally.
Whether players identify the most dangerous opponent.
Whether communication increases during the repeat entry.
Whether defenders retain structure under fatigue.
Whether the second exit decision improves.
progressions: Introduce a third entry if the second exit fails.
Reduce recovery time between footballs.
Add full match-like tackling.
Begin with different scoreboard and time situations.
Require the defence to retain possession after exiting.
regressions: Allow five seconds before the second entry.
successIndicators: React immediately to a failed exit.
Defend repeated entries without losing composure.
Improve the exit decision after the second stop.
matchApplication: Repeat entries are among the most demanding defensive phases in Australian football. This drill develops the communication, recovery running and structural discipline required when a team’s first attempt to leave defensive 50 fails.

title: Defensive Communication Chain
primarySkill: Providing clear, continuous defensive information across multiple lines.
objective: Develop a consistent communication system that allows defenders to organise pressure, cover, opponents, space and movement before dangerous situations develop.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with target gates at each end.
Divide the defending team into a front, middle and deep line.
Nominate one communicator in each line.
Teach the approved calls:
“Ball” for the pressure defender
“Inside” for corridor protection
“Back” for a player behind the defensive line
“Switch” for movement to the opposite side
“Hold” for maintaining shape
“Step” for moving the line forward
The attacking team begins with possession.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football through the area.
The defensive team must organise its movement using the approved calls.
The deepest communicator identifies opponents and space that teammates cannot see.
The middle communicator transfers that information to the front line.
The front line communicates pressure and the direction of the ball carrier.
The coach awards the defence one communication point when correct information changes a teammate’s action.
Defenders also score through intercepts, forced backwards disposals and turnovers.
Change the nominated communicators after each block.
coachingPoints: Communication must be early, specific and connected to an action.
Use names wherever possible.
The deepest players have the widest view and must provide information continuously.
Do not use several different words for the same instruction.
Players receiving information must acknowledge and act on it.
Communicate before opponents move into dangerous space.
Avoid commentary that does not help a teammate make a decision.
Leadership responsibility should rotate across the group.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether communication occurs before the danger develops.
Whether players use the approved calls consistently.
Whether information travels from the deepest line forward.
Whether teammates respond to instructions.
Whether quiet players become involved when given responsibility.
Whether communication remains clear under pressure.
progressions: Remove the nominated communicators.
Add full tackling.
Increase attacking speed.
Award bonus points for preventing a score through communication.
Introduce crowd noise or controlled distractions.
regressions: Pause after each disposal to identify required information.
Allow the coach to model the communication.
successIndicators: Organise opponents, space and defensive roles without coach intervention.
matchApplication: Effective team defence depends on players sharing information that teammates cannot see. This drill establishes a common communication system for pressure, cover, switches, loose opponents and line movement.

title: Defensive Shape Through Switch Play
primarySkill: Maintaining defensive shape through repeated opposition switches.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to slide, hold central protection and identify the correct moment to pressure during repeated switches of play.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground using the full width.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use two-thirds of the ground and mark three vertical lanes: left, corridor and right.
Position the attacking team across the full width.
Arrange the defence in connected front, middle and deep lines.
Place attacking scoring gates at the far end.
Begin with the attack controlling possession on one wing.
Require the attack to complete at least one switch before attempting to score during the first phase.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football across the width of the ground.
The defence slides as a connected unit while continuing to protect the corridor.
Ball-side defenders pressure short options.
Weak-side defenders move into central cover rather than remaining on the far boundary.
When the attack switches, the defence exchanges pressure and cover responsibilities.
Defenders may press aggressively if the switch is slow, inaccurate or received by a stationary player.
Attackers score by moving through a target gate.
Defenders score one point for forcing another switch, two points for an intercept and three points for a turnover followed by a successful exit.
coachingPoints: Move as the switch is being prepared, not after it is completed.
Protect the corridor throughout the lateral movement.
The weak-side line must remain connected enough to reach the next receiver.
Do not chase every disposal at maximum speed.
Recognise when to slide, hold or press.
Maintain depth behind the ball-side pressure.
Communicate the likely switch from the deepest line.
Recover central balance after applying wide pressure.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defence begins moving before the football travels.
Whether central space remains protected.
Whether weak-side defenders become too wide.
Whether pressure is applied selectively.
Whether the lines remain connected across the width.
Whether defenders recover central balance after pressing.
progressions: Remove the required switch rule.
Add full tackling.
Allow attackers to use long kicks over defensive lines.
Begin from rapid turnovers.
Introduce a time limit for the attacking score.
regressions: Use handball and short kicks only.
Mark defensive reference positions with cones.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor throughout lateral movement.
Recognise poor switches as pressure opportunities.
Prevent repeated switches from opening an uncontested central route.
matchApplication: Opposition teams use switches to stretch defensive structures and create space through the corridor. This drill teaches defenders to move collectively across the ground without becoming disconnected or overcommitting to harmless wide possession.

title: Team Defence Fundamentals Assessment
primarySkill: Applying foundational team-defence principles in an integrated game environment.
objective: Assess whether players can independently apply the foundational team-defence principles introduced in TD-001 to TD-019 during continuous, realistic play.
groundSize: Two-thirds to full ground, depending on player numbers.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two-thirds or the full ground with normal goals at one end.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
Position the defence in realistic forward, midfield and deep defensive lines.
Place two wide and two central defensive exit gates.
Prepare a sequence of starting scenarios:
Slow opposition possession
Fast turnover
Wide switch
Outnumbered attack
Forward entry
Failed defensive exit
Assign assistant coaches or leaders to observe specific defensive principles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each repetition from one of the prepared scenarios.
The attacking team attempts to score using unrestricted football.
The defending team must establish shape, protect dangerous space and apply coordinated pressure.
After a defensive stop, the team attempts to exit through an appropriate gate.
If the exit fails, the coach immediately begins a repeat entry.
Each repetition continues for 45–90 seconds before resetting.
Coaches assess the defence against the nominated success criteria.
Teams swap roles after six repetitions and complete the same scenarios.
coachingPoints: Establish goal-side and central protection immediately.
Maintain connected lines behind the football.
Identify pressure, cover and balance roles around possession.
Force opposition movement towards less dangerous areas.
Communicate opponents, switches, pressure triggers and space behind the play.
Delay when outnumbered and press when support is available.
Reset immediately after failed exits or repeat entries.
Secure possession and select an appropriate defensive exit.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How quickly the team establishes defensive shape.
Whether defenders remain goal-side.
Whether the corridor and top of defensive 50 are protected.
Whether pressure is supported by cover and balance.
Whether defensive lines remain connected.
Whether communication is early and specific.
Whether the team delays correctly when outnumbered.
Whether players reset after repeat entries.
Whether the first exit decision suits the pressure.
Whether the group adapts without direct coach instruction.
progressions: Remove all coach-directed starting information.
Use full match-like contact.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
Require the defence to transition from the exit into a forward entry.
Allow the attacking team to plan its own method for breaking the defensive structure.
regressions: Assess one defensive principle at a time.
Use half-ground rather than two-thirds or full-ground.
Allow defensive leaders to organise the group before each restart.
successIndicators: Establish a connected shape within three seconds of the starting action.
Protect the corridor and central scoring areas.
Recognise and act on pressing triggers.
Secure the defensive stop and select an appropriate exit.
Apply the principles without constant coach direction.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the foundational team-defence behaviours required in Australian football. It measures whether players can organise collectively, protect dangerous space, respond to changing attacking methods, win possession and transition safely out of defence.

title: Defensive Shuffle and Close
primarySkill: Closing space while maintaining balanced defensive footwork.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to move laterally, close an opponent under control and influence the direction of the next disposal without losing balance.
groundSize: 20 metres long × 15 metres wide per working group.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Mark two parallel movement lanes approximately five metres apart.
Place an attacker with a football at one end of each lane.
Position a defender three to five metres away and slightly goal-side.
Place a receiver at the far end of the area.
Run multiple groups simultaneously where player numbers allow.
Begin at controlled speed before increasing intensity.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker moves laterally between the two lanes while carrying the football.
The defender mirrors the movement using short, balanced adjustment steps.
On the coach’s signal, the attacker attempts to move forward and dispose to the receiver.
The defender closes space from an angle that removes the attacker’s preferred inside option.
The defender applies controlled pressure without tackling during the introductory phase.
The attacker must dispose within three seconds of the signal.
Rotate the attacker, defender and receiver after each repetition.
Award the defender one point for forcing a wide or inaccurate disposal and two points for a legal smother or intercept.
coachingPoints: Maintain a low, balanced stance while moving laterally.
Use short adjustment steps rather than crossing the feet.
Keep the hips open enough to react in either direction.
Close space under control and avoid running past the attacker.
Approach from the side that removes the most dangerous disposal.
Watch the attacker’s hips and football position rather than reacting only to head movement.
Accelerate during the final two to three steps of the close.
Finish close enough to affect the disposal while remaining balanced.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders cross their feet while shuffling.
Whether their body position allows movement in both directions.
Whether the closing angle removes the dangerous option.
Whether defenders decelerate before reaching the attacker.
Whether pressure affects the quality or direction of the disposal.
Whether players remain goal-side throughout the movement.
progressions: Allow the attacker to change direction twice before advancing.
Introduce full legal tackling.
Add a second receiver to create a disposal decision.
Reduce the starting distance between attacker and defender.
Begin with the defender recovering from behind.
regressions: Remove the disposal and focus only on movement technique.
successIndicators: Move laterally without crossing their feet.
Maintain balance through changes of direction.
Close space from an effective angle.
Influence the attacker towards a less dangerous disposal.
matchApplication: Balanced defensive footwork allows players to close ball carriers, protect the corridor and react to changes of direction without conceding an easy escape. It is fundamental to applying pressure around contests and in open play.

title: Tracking and Releasing a Running Opponent
primarySkill: Tracking an opponent through one defensive area and handing responsibility to a teammate.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to track an opponent’s movement, communicate a controlled handover and return to protecting their own defensive space.
groundSize: 35 metres long × 25 metres wide, divided into three horizontal zones.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Divide the playing area into three horizontal defensive zones.
Position one or two defenders in each zone.
Place attackers at one end and a feeder outside the area.
Attackers run through multiple zones before presenting as a receiving option.
Defenders may track an attacker within their zone but must communicate before responsibility changes.
Position a scoring gate at the attacking end.
howTheDrillWorks:
An attacker begins a run from the first zone towards the scoring gate.
The first defender tracks goal-side while the attacker remains in their area.
As the attacker approaches the next zone, the first defender calls the handover.
The defender in the next zone accepts responsibility and continues tracking.
The releasing defender returns to a central position in their original zone.
The feeder may dispose to the runner at any point.
Defenders attempt to intercept, spoil or force possession away from the scoring gate.
Rotate attackers and defenders after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Track the opponent from a goal-side and inside position.
Communicate before the opponent enters the next defensive area.
Use the teammate’s name and a clear location call.
Do not release responsibility until the next defender acknowledges the handover.
After releasing, return immediately to the most dangerous space.
The accepting defender must adjust body position before the opponent arrives.
Maintain awareness of both the football and the runner.
Avoid two defenders following the same opponent through multiple zones.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders track from the correct side.
Whether the handover call occurs early enough.
Whether the next defender acknowledges responsibility.
Whether the releasing defender returns to central space.
Whether attackers become free between zones.
Whether defenders retain vision of the football.
progressions: Add a second crossing runner.
Remove the visible zone lines.
Allow the feeder to use kicks of different lengths.
Introduce controlled body contact.
Add a stationary attacker who occupies a defender in the next zone.
regressions: Use one runner at a time.
Pause play at each handover point.
successIndicators: Track runners from a goal-side position.
Communicate before the handover is required.
Return to protecting their own space after releasing.
Prevent uncontested possession between defensive zones.
matchApplication: Midfielders and forwards regularly run through multiple defensive lines. This drill teaches defenders when to follow, when to hand over and how to avoid being dragged away from the space they are responsible for protecting.

title: Recovery Arc to Goal Side
primarySkill: Recovering through an inside arc to regain goal-side positioning.
objective: Teach beaten defenders to recover through the shortest inside route, protect the scoring line and re-enter the contest from a useful defensive position.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a scoring gate at one end of the area.
Position an attacker with a football approximately 20 metres from the gate.
Place a defender two metres outside and slightly behind the attacker.
Use cones to mark an inside recovery arc towards the scoring gate.
Position a second attacker or feeder near the starting line.
Run several lanes simultaneously where possible.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker begins moving towards the scoring gate.
The defender starts from a beaten outside position.
The defender sprints along the inside recovery arc rather than following directly behind.
The defender attempts to regain a position between the attacker and the gate.
The attacker may carry the football or receive from the feeder.
Once goal-side, the defender applies controlled pressure and attempts to force the attacker wide.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
Award the defender one point for regaining goal-side position and two points for preventing a score.
coachingPoints: Turn and accelerate immediately when beaten.
Recover towards the scoring line rather than following the opponent’s path.
Use the shortest inside angle available.
Do not look continuously at the attacker while sprinting; check position with quick glances.
Re-enter the contest under control.
Once goal-side, reduce speed and adopt balanced defensive footwork.
Communicate with teammates who may be delaying the attack.
Continue defending even if the original opponent passes the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders choose the inside recovery line.
Whether acceleration begins immediately.
Whether defenders regain goal-side position before applying pressure.
Whether players lose speed by watching the opponent continuously.
Whether the defender arrives under control.
Whether pressure then forces the attacker wide.
progressions: Add a second attacker to create a recovery decision.
Increase the starting deficit.
Introduce a live tackle once goal-side position is regained.
Allow the attacker to change direction.
Begin from a turnover rather than a stationary start.
regressions: Start the defender level with the attacker.
Remove the football and focus on running lines.
successIndicators: Arrive balanced enough to apply pressure.
Prevent or delay the scoring opportunity.
matchApplication: Defenders are regularly beaten during turnovers, forward entries and overlap play. Recovering through the inside protects the shortest route to goal and allows the defender to rejoin the contest rather than chasing ineffectively from behind.

title: Defending the Give-and-Go
primarySkill: Defending a ball carrier who disposes and immediately runs to receive again.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to maintain pressure on the football while tracking the original ball carrier’s continued run after disposal.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with a scoring gate at one end.
Begin with two attackers against two defenders.
One attacker starts with the football and the other begins five to eight metres ahead.
Match each attacker with a defender.
The ball carrier is encouraged to dispose and continue running.
Rotate pairs after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first attacker disposes to the supporting attacker and continues running forward.
The first defender pressures the initial disposal and then tracks the continuing runner.
The second defender pressures the new ball carrier.
Defenders communicate whether to stay with opponents or exchange responsibilities.
The attackers attempt to complete the return handball and score through the target gate.
Defenders score one point for preventing the return possession and two points for a turnover.
If the give-and-go succeeds, defenders recover through the inside and continue the contest.
Reset from the opposite side after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Do not stop defending when the opponent disposes of the football.
Track the original ball carrier’s continuing run.
The second defender must pressure the new ball carrier and reduce the return-handball window.
Communicate whether defenders are staying or switching.
Protect the inside route to the scoring gate.
Position in the passing lane without losing awareness of the football.
If the return handball is completed, recover through goal-side space.
Maintain legal pressure without obstructing the runner.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first defender stops after the initial disposal.
Whether the return passing lane is protected.
Whether the second defender pressures the receiver.
Whether defenders communicate switches.
Whether the running attacker is forced wider.
Whether recovery continues after a successful give-and-go.
progressions: Add a third attacker providing a second return option.
Allow the attackers to kick as well as handball.
Introduce full legal tackling.
Begin at greater speed from a turnover.
Remove predetermined match-ups.
regressions: Use walking pace during the first repetitions.
successIndicators: Continue defending after an opponent disposes.
Track the original ball carrier’s run.
Apply pressure to the new ball carrier.
Deny or delay the return possession.
Recover goal-side if the combination succeeds.
matchApplication: Give-and-go handballs allow players to break defensive lines through continued movement. Defenders must recognise that the original ball carrier remains dangerous after disposal and coordinate pressure on both the football and the runner.

title: Sliding Line Against Lateral Ball Movement
primarySkill: Moving a defensive line laterally while maintaining spacing and depth.
objective: Develop the coordinated lateral movement required for a defensive line to follow ball movement without creating gaps or losing central protection.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Divide the width of the area into left, central and right lanes.
Position the attacking team across one end of the area.
Arrange the defenders in one connected horizontal line approximately 10–12 metres from the attackers.
Place three scoring gates behind the defensive line.
Begin with the football in one outside lane.
Nominate the deepest or central defender as the line organiser.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football laterally between lanes.
The defensive line slides together towards the football.
The nearest defender applies controlled pressure while the remaining defenders preserve spacing.
Weak-side defenders move towards the centre without completely abandoning the far lane.
The attack may attempt to pass through a scoring gate when a gap appears.
Defenders score one point for forcing a backwards disposal and two points for an intercept.
The coach may call “freeze” to assess line spacing and depth.
Teams swap roles after three-minute blocks.
coachingPoints: Move when the ball carrier prepares to dispose.
Maintain consistent spacing between defenders.
Avoid having one player advance while the rest remain flat.
Protect the central gate before the far-side gate.
The nearest defender presses while the line behind remains connected.
Weak-side defenders should narrow towards central cover.
Adjust both laterally and slightly forward or backward according to the ball carrier’s time.
Communicate the direction and speed of the slide.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the line begins moving before the disposal.
Whether spacing remains consistent.
Whether the nearest defender separates too far from teammates.
Whether weak-side players narrow appropriately.
Whether the central gate remains protected.
Whether the line adjusts depth as well as width.
progressions: Remove the marked lanes.
Add live tackling.
Allow the attack to use long kicks over the line.
Introduce a forward positioned behind the defence.
Begin from rapid changes of possession.
regressions: Predetermine the direction of ball movement.
Reduce the number of attacking gates.
Mark maximum spacing between defenders with cones.
successIndicators: Adjust width and depth before the attacking disposal is completed.
matchApplication: Defensive lines must move across the ground as opposition possession changes sides. A connected slide prevents attackers from accessing gaps between defenders and ensures central space remains protected during lateral ball movement.

title: Defending the Lead-Up Chain
primarySkill: Defending consecutive lead-up receivers through multiple areas.
objective: Develop coordinated defensive movement against an attack using repeated short leads to advance the football through connected receivers.
groundSize: 55 metres long × 30 metres wide, divided into three sections.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the playing area into three consecutive sections.
Position two attackers and two defenders in each section.
The attacking team begins at one end with the football.
Attackers attempt to advance through a series of short lead-up possessions.
Defenders begin goal-side of their direct opponents.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
howTheDrillWorks:
An attacker in the first section leads and receives the football.
The defender closes the receiver and attempts to force a backwards or wide disposal.
Attackers in the next section begin their leads as the receiver gains possession.
Defenders communicate whether to track, switch or hand over the next runner.
The attacking team attempts to complete one possession in each section before scoring.
Defenders score one point for forcing a backwards disposal and two points for an intercept or spoil.
After a turnover, defenders attempt to move the football back through the starting line.
