Allow defensive leaders to organise before each restart.
successIndicators: Apply pressure without losing team structure.
Protect the ball carrier’s release options.
Recover spills created by defensive contests.
Win possession safely and complete an organised exit.
Maintain communication and legal technique under fatigue.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the pressure and contest behaviours required to create turnovers in Australian football. It measures whether players can tackle, spoil, smother, defend congestion and recover loose footballs while preserving the wider defensive structure.

title: Second-Defender Tackle Assist
primarySkill: Timing a second-defender tackle assist without releasing another dangerous opponent.
objective: Develop players’ ability to decide when a second defender should assist a tackle and when they must remain outside the contest to protect the next disposal.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with a target gate at each end.
Begin with two attackers against three defenders.
One attacker starts with the football while the second provides a nearby release option.
Position one defender as the primary tackler, one as the potential assist defender and one as deeper balance.
The assist defender begins between the ball carrier and the release option.
Rotate all players through each role.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier attempts to move through the target gate.
The primary defender closes and applies a legal tackle.
The assist defender initially protects the release option.
The assist defender may join the tackle only when the ball carrier remains upright, the release option is covered and assistance is required.
The balance defender protects behind the contest and prepares for a spill.
If the ball carrier releases, defenders immediately rotate pressure and cover responsibilities.
Defenders score one point for forcing an ineffective disposal and two points for winning possession.
Reset after a score, turnover or stoppage.
coachingPoints: The second defender must assess the tackle before committing.
Protect the release option until assistance is genuinely required.
Join from a legal angle and avoid high or dangerous contact.
Do not allow both defenders to finish on the ground.
The balance defender must remain goal-side.
Communicate “assist”, “release” or “hold”.
Expect the football to spill when additional pressure arrives.
Rotate immediately if the ball carrier disposes successfully.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the second defender protects the release before assisting.
Whether the tackle genuinely requires help.
Whether legal contact technique is maintained.
Whether another attacker becomes free.
Whether a defender remains behind the contest.
Whether players recover the spilled football.
progressions: Add a third attacking release option.
Permit full match-like tackling.
Begin from a contested ground ball.
Allow the ball carrier to kick or handball.
Require an immediate defensive exit after possession is won.
regressions: Predetermine when the second defender must assist.
Use tackle bags before live contact.
Use touch pressure and focus on positioning.
successIndicators: Recognise when tackle assistance is required.
Join the tackle legally and effectively.
Preserve a balance defender behind the contest.
Win or neutralise possession without releasing a free attacker.
matchApplication: A second defender can strengthen a tackle and prevent an effective disposal, but joining unnecessarily may free an opposition player. This drill develops the judgement required to balance tackle assistance with protection of the next possession.

title: Ground-Ball Squeeze and Release Denial
primarySkill: Compressing around a ground-ball contest while denying clean release options.
objective: Develop a connected defensive squeeze around a loose football that pressures the collector while protecting the first outside release.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a square area with one exit gate on each side.
Place three attackers and three defenders around a central loose football.
Position one attacker closest to the football and two as outside release options.
Defenders begin with one contest player, one release-lane defender and one balance defender.
The coach varies the direction and speed of the ground-ball release.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach rolls the football into the centre.
The nearest attacker attempts to collect and release to a teammate.
The first defender pressures the collector.
The second defender positions in the most likely handball lane.
The third defender remains goal-side and protects the opposite release or loose spill.
If possession changes, defenders may exit through any gate.
Defenders score one point for forcing a stoppage and two points for winning possession.
Attackers score by completing possession through an exit gate.
coachingPoints: Pressure the collector without diving past the football.
Protect the likely release before joining the contest.
Maintain one defender outside the congestion.
Close space from several angles rather than one straight line.
Accept a stoppage when clean possession cannot be won.
Communicate which exit is protected.
Keep feet active and body position strong.
Spread quickly after winning possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the collector is pressured immediately.
Whether release lanes remain protected.
Whether all defenders become trapped in congestion.
Whether players remain goal-side.
Whether the football is forced into a stoppage or turnover.
Whether the defence spreads after winning possession.
progressions: Add a fourth attacker as an outside receiver.
Reduce the area.
Introduce full tackling.
Begin with the football bouncing unpredictably.
Continue into a larger transition area after the defensive exit.
regressions: Begin with the defence holding numerical advantage.
successIndicators: Force congestion, a stoppage or a turnover.
matchApplication: Ground-ball contests are often decided by the players positioned around the collector rather than by the first player to reach the football. This drill develops the pressure and release-lane protection required to prevent a clean opposition escape.

title: Influenced Kick Intercept Channel
primarySkill: Using pressure on the kicker to direct the disposal into a prepared intercept area.
objective: Develop coordination between the defender pressuring the kicker and teammates positioned to intercept the predictable disposal created by that pressure.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with left, central and right channels.
Position a ball carrier at one end with three possible receivers ahead.
Place one pressure defender near the kicker.
Position two cover defenders in the likely disposal channels.
Nominate one channel as the preferred defensive intercept area.
Rotate pressure, cover and attacking roles after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier receives and attempts to kick to one of three receivers.
The pressure defender closes from an angle that removes the safest central option.
Cover defenders protect the short and dangerous alternatives.
The remaining channel is deliberately left as the least damaging option.
An intercept defender reads the pressured kick and attacks that channel.
Defenders score one point for directing the kick into the planned channel and two points for an intercept.
After an intercept, the defence attempts to exit through a wide gate.
Reset with a new preferred intercept channel.
coachingPoints: Pressure must influence the direction of the kick.
Close the kicker’s preferred side without running past.
Cover defenders must remove realistic alternatives.
The intercept player should position with depth to move forward.
Communicate the channel being offered.
Do not leave a central scoring option open.
Read the kicker’s hips, shoulders and ball position.
Spread immediately after an intercept.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the pressure angle influences the kicker.
Whether cover defenders remove the correct options.
Whether the offered kick is genuinely less dangerous.
Whether the interceptor reads the disposal early.
Whether defenders attack the ball rather than wait underneath it.
Whether transition begins immediately after possession is won.
progressions: Allow the ball carrier to run and carry.
Remove the nominated intercept channel.
Add full tackling.
Introduce a switch before the pressured kick.
Require the intercept to lead to a forward entry.
regressions: Mark the intercept position with cones.
successIndicators: Influence the direction of the kick.
Direct possession into a planned low-value area.
Read and attack the pressured disposal.
matchApplication: Intercepts are often created by coordinated pressure rather than individual anticipation alone. A defender can shape the kicker’s options while teammates position to win the predictable disposal.

title: Spoil-to-Safety Directional Defence
primarySkill: Directing a spoil towards safe space or defensive support.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to control the direction of an aerial spoil so the football moves away from goal and towards supporting teammates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position a feeder 25–35 metres from an aerial contest.
Place one attacker and one defender in the contest.
Mark two safety zones wide of the contest and a scoring gate behind it.
Position defensive support players in or near the safety zones.
Place attacking crumbers around the front of the contest.
Rotate all players through aerial and ground-level roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder kicks towards the aerial contest.
The defender attempts to mark or spoil.
If marking is unlikely, the defender directs the spoil towards a nominated safety zone.
Supporting defenders attack the expected spoil area.
Attacking crumbers attempt to win possession and score.
Defenders score one point for a spoil away from goal and two points for a spoil recovered by a teammate.
A spoil directly towards goal gives the attacking team a bonus point.
Reset after the football is secured, scored or leaves the area.
coachingPoints: Establish goal-side body position before the football arrives.
Judge whether to mark or spoil early.
Use the correct hand and body angle to direct the spoil.
Avoid bringing the football back into the corridor.
Ground-level support must move while the kick is in flight.
Communicate the intended spoil direction.
Retain one defender behind the contest.
Secure possession before beginning the exit.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender gains effective aerial position.
Whether the spoil direction is controlled.
Whether support players anticipate the safety zone.
Whether attacking crumbers are goal-side.
Whether one defender protects behind the contest.
Whether the defence wins the second possession.
progressions: Add a second aerial attacker.
Remove the nominated safety zone.
Vary kick height and direction.
Introduce full match-like body contact.
Add a repeat entry if the defensive recovery fails.
successIndicators: Position support in the expected spill area.
Recover the second possession or force a stoppage.
matchApplication: An effective spoil should not simply stop a mark; it should move the football towards safer space. Directional spoiling allows defenders to control the next contest and reduces the chance of an immediate opposition score.

title: Crumb-to-Tackle Defensive Chain
primarySkill: Applying immediate tackle pressure when the opposition wins the crumb from an aerial contest.
objective: Develop the defensive reaction required when an attacking crumber wins possession, ensuring the receiver is tackled or pressured before creating a scoring opportunity.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position a feeder outside a contested marking area.
Place one attacker and one defender in the aerial contest.
Position two attacking crumbers and three ground-level defenders.
Place a scoring gate behind the contest and two defensive exit gates wide.
Nominate one ground defender as the first crumb-pressure player.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder kicks to the aerial contest.
The aerial defender attempts to mark or spoil.
If an attacker wins the crumb, the nearest ground defender applies immediate tackle pressure.
The second defender closes the likely release handball.
The third defender protects goal-side space.
If the defence wins possession, it exits through a wide gate.
Defenders score one point for preventing a clean shot and two points for a turnover and exit.
Attackers score by moving the football through the central gate.
coachingPoints: Ground defenders must move before the spill occurs.
The nearest player pressures the crumb winner immediately.
The second defender protects the release rather than joining the tackle.
Maintain a defender between the contest and goal.
Close under control and tackle legally.
If the ball spills again, reset pressure, cover and balance roles.
Communicate which attacker is front and centre.
Secure the defensive win before exiting.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders anticipate the ground-ball location.
Whether the crumb winner is pressured immediately.
Whether release options are protected.
Whether a goal-side defender remains behind.
Whether tackle technique remains legal.
Whether the defence reacts to a second spill.
progressions: Add a third attacking crumber.
Allow the feeder to vary the kick.
Introduce full match-like contact.
Add a second entry if the defensive exit fails.
Require the defence to progress into a forward entry after exiting.
successIndicators: Protect the release and goal-side space.
matchApplication: Even when an aerial contest is defended successfully, the opposition may win the ground ball. Immediate pressure on the crumber prevents a clean snap, handball or central release.

title: Pressure the Receiver on Arrival
primarySkill: Closing a receiver as possession arrives to prevent forward continuation.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to arrive with controlled pressure as an opponent receives possession, preventing the receiver from turning, accelerating or disposing effectively.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with a target gate at each end.
Position a feeder with two possible receivers ahead.
Place a defender three to five metres from each receiver.
Receivers may lead forward, laterally or back towards the feeder.
Defenders begin goal-side and must read the feeder’s disposal.
Rotate feeding, attacking and defending roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receivers move to create a passing option.
The feeder selects one receiver and disposes by kick or handball.
The defender closes while the football is travelling.
The defender aims to arrive as possession is taken.
If the receiver plays on, controlled tackling becomes live.
The receiver attempts to move through the target gate or release to the second attacker.
Defenders score one point for forcing a backwards disposal and two points for a turnover.
Reset with receivers changing starting positions.
coachingPoints: Read the feeder’s body position before the disposal.
Begin closing as the football is released.
Arrive close enough to prevent the receiver turning.
Decelerate during the final steps.
Maintain goal-side position.
Close the receiver’s preferred disposal side.
Do not make early contact before possession is established.
Recover immediately if the receiver releases the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders read the disposal early.
Whether closing begins during the football’s travel.
Whether players arrive balanced.
Whether receivers are prevented from turning forward.
Whether pressure influences the next disposal.
Whether defenders continue after the ball is released.
progressions: Add a third receiver.
Allow the feeder to use longer kicks.
Introduce full tackling after play on.
Reduce the defender’s starting distance.
Continue play through multiple consecutive receivers.
successIndicators: Read the disposal before it arrives.
Force sideways, backwards or ineffective disposals.
matchApplication: Defensive pressure is most effective when it arrives with the football. Closing late allows opponents to turn and accelerate, while arriving under control can stop forward momentum and force a predictable disposal.

title: Contest-to-Contest Defensive Repeat
primarySkill: Reorganising and applying pressure across consecutive contests.
objective: Develop players’ ability to complete one defensive contest, recover immediately and establish pressure, cover and balance around the next contest.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 35 metres wide, divided into three contest zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into three consecutive contest zones.
Position attackers and defenders in each zone.
Begin with a ground-ball or aerial contest in the first zone.
The coach holds spare footballs to initiate the next phase.
After each contest, selected defenders must move forward or fold behind into the next zone.
Rotate players through all three zones.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first contest begins from a coach-directed football.
Once possession is resolved, the coach immediately starts a second contest in the next zone.
Defenders from the completed contest recover and join the next phase.
The nearest player becomes pressure, the second provides cover and the third holds balance.
A third contest begins immediately after the second phase.
Defenders score one point for each stopped attack and three points for winning all three phases.
Attackers score by exiting through the final gate.
Complete work blocks of 45–60 seconds before rotating.
coachingPoints: Do not remain at a completed contest.
Recover through the shortest useful route.
Identify the next pressure, cover and balance roles while moving.
Communicate which defenders are arriving.
Avoid having every player chase the football.
Maintain legal contact technique under fatigue.
Fold behind when the next contest moves away.
Finish each phase before preparing to exit.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders react immediately to the next contest.
Whether recovery routes are efficient.
Whether roles are established before arrival.
Whether defensive structure survives repeated effort.
Whether players communicate while fatigued.
Whether contact remains controlled and legal.
progressions: Reduce time between contests.
Use full match-like contact.
Add a fourth contest phase.
Begin each phase from an unpredictable location.
Require a controlled exit after the final defensive win.
successIndicators: Complete several defensive efforts without losing discipline.
matchApplication: Australian football regularly involves several contests in rapid succession. Defenders must leave completed actions, recover around the football and contribute to the next phase before the opposition can escape.

title: Boundary Stoppage Lock-In
primarySkill: Preventing the opposition from escaping a boundary stoppage into central space.
objective: Develop a defensive structure that uses the boundary to restrict space, pressures the first possession and denies an opposition exit towards the corridor.
groundSize: 30 metres long × 25 metres wide beside a boundary line.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a stoppage area beside the boundary.
Place one attacking exit gate towards the corridor and one further along the boundary.
Position equal numbers around a throw-in simulation.
Defenders nominate first-possession pressure, inside cover and rear balance roles.
The corridor gate is worth more than the boundary-side exit.
Rotate stoppage positions regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach throws the football into the stoppage.
The attacking team attempts to win possession and exit through either gate.
The nearest defender pressures the first possession.
Inside defenders protect the corridor exit.
The balance defender remains behind the stoppage and covers a backward release.
Defenders may concede movement further along the boundary while denying the inside escape.
Defenders score one point for forcing a repeat stoppage and two points for a turnover.
Attackers score three points through the corridor gate and one point along the boundary.
coachingPoints: Protect the inside exit before attacking the football.
Use the boundary to reduce available space.
Pressure the first possession immediately.
Keep one defender outside the stoppage as balance.
Do not allow a clean backward handball into the corridor.
Communicate whether the football is inside, outside or behind.
Accept a repeat stoppage as a successful defensive result.
Reset quickly after the football leaves the immediate contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the corridor exit is protected.
Whether the first possession receives pressure.
Whether all defenders become drawn into the stoppage.
Whether the backward release is covered.
Whether the attack is forced along the boundary.
Whether defenders reset after the first clearance.

Allow unrestricted tackling.
Continue play into a larger area after the exit.
Vary the throw-in depth.
Introduce a late attacking runner from behind.

Force the opposition along the boundary.

matchApplication: Boundary stoppages provide a strong opportunity to contain the opposition because one side of the contest is already closed. The defence must protect the inside release and avoid allowing a clean exit into the corridor.

title: Forward-Entry Contest Denial Wave
primarySkill: Defending repeated forward entries through coordinated contest pressure and ground-level support.
objective: Develop a defensive unit capable of contesting repeated inside-50 entries, controlling the spill and resetting quickly when the opposition retains possession.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the attacking half of the ground.
Position attackers across half-forward and inside 50.
Arrange defenders in high, aerial, ground-level and goal-side roles.
Place spare footballs with coaches around the 50-metre arc.
Place two wide and one central defensive exit gate.
Explain that another football may be introduced if the first entry is spoiled but not cleared.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with a forward entry.
Defenders contest the aerial ball and organise around the expected spill.
If the attackers retain possession, they immediately deliver another entry.
Defenders must reset match-ups, protect front-and-centre space and communicate the next contest.
The phase continues for up to three entries.
Defenders score one point for each stopped entry and three points for a successful controlled exit.
Attackers score for goals or uncontested marks inside the scoring zone.
Rotate positional roles after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Pressure the player delivering the forward entry.
Aerial defenders must protect goal-side position.
Ground defenders should organise before the football arrives.
Protect front-and-centre and the back of the contest.
Reset immediately if the opposition retains possession.
Reassign opponents based on danger rather than original match-ups.
Maintain communication across repeated entries.
Use a composed exit after the defensive win.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether pressure influences the entry kick.
Whether aerial defenders gain goal-side position.
Whether ground-level roles are organised.
Whether defenders reset after incomplete clearances.
Whether dangerous opponents are reassigned.

title: Advanced Pressure and Contest Assessment
primarySkill: Applying advanced defensive pressure and contest principles during continuous match-like play.
objective: Assess whether players can independently combine the advanced pressure and contest behaviours developed through TD-051 to TD-059 across changing field positions and repeated phases.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two-thirds or the full ground.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
Prepare the following starting scenarios:
Ball carrier under tackle pressure with a nearby release
Loose ground ball with outside support
Pressured kick into an intercept channel
Aerial contest requiring a directional spoil
Attacking crumb inside 50
Boundary stoppage
Repeat forward entries
Position coaches to assess pressure, cover, balance, communication and legal contact.
Rotate teams after completing all scenarios.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each repetition from one prepared scenario.
The attacking team attempts to retain possession, exit or score.
The defence must apply the correct pressure and contest response without prior instruction.
All spills, smothers, tackles and spoils remain live.
If the attacking team retains possession, the phase continues into another contest.
After winning possession, defenders attempt a controlled exit.
Each repetition lasts 60–120 seconds.
Complete six to eight repetitions before exchanging roles.
coachingPoints: Decide whether the second defender should assist the tackle or protect the release.
Compress around ground balls without losing outside balance.
Use pressure to shape opposition disposals.
Direct spoils away from goal and towards support.
Pressure attacking crumbers immediately.
Close receivers as possession arrives.
Reorganise between consecutive contests.
Protect the corridor at boundary stoppages.
Reset after repeated forward entries.
Maintain safe, legal and disciplined contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether tackle assistance is used appropriately.
Whether release lanes remain protected.
Whether the defence retains balance around ground-ball contests.
Whether pressure influences kicks and handballs.
Whether spoils are directed towards safe space.
Whether crumbers and receivers are pressured immediately.
Whether players recover into the next contest.
Whether boundary exits are denied.
Whether repeated entries are defended with structure.
Whether defensive wins lead to composed exits.
progressions: Remove all coach explanation before each scenario.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure consequences.

Require the defensive exit to develop into a complete forward entry.

regressions: Assess one scenario at a time.
Use controlled rather than match-like contact.
Allow defensive organisation before each restart.
Shorten the work periods and increase recovery.
successIndicators: Apply the correct pressure response to each scenario.
Protect release options while contesting possession.
Maintain balance around ground balls and tackles.
Influence opposition disposals towards defensive support.
Communicate throughout congested and open phases.
Preserve legal contact technique under fatigue.
Win possession and complete an appropriate exit.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the advanced pressure and contest behaviours required throughout Australian football. It measures whether players can create turnovers through coordinated tackling, ground-ball pressure, influenced disposals, controlled spoiling and repeat defensive effort while preserving the wider team structure.

title: Backline-to-Midfield Screen Connection
primarySkill: Connecting the defensive line with a midfield screen in front of the football.
objective: Develop coordinated movement between defenders and midfielders so the space in front of defensive 50 remains protected against short passes, central leads and forward-running opponents.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line, using approximately two-thirds of the ground width.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position a backline inside defensive 50 and a midfield defensive screen 15–20 metres higher.
Place attackers across half-forward, the corridor and inside 50.
Begin with the attacking team controlling possession near the centre square.
Mark a central protection zone between the arcs.
Place two wide exit gates for the defending team.
Nominate one communicator in the backline and one in the midfield screen.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football across half-forward and attempts to enter inside 50.
The midfield screen protects short central options and pressures the ball carrier.
The backline maintains suitable depth behind the screen and tracks deeper forwards.
If an attacker moves between the two defensive lines, responsibility is communicated and handed over.
The defence attempts to force the entry wide or intercept the football.
After winning possession, defenders connect with the midfield screen before exiting through a wide gate.
Defenders score one point for forcing a wide entry, two points for an intercept and three points for a controlled exit.
Teams change roles after four-minute blocks.
coachingPoints: Maintain 15–20 metres between the midfield screen and the backline.
Midfielders must protect the space in front of the deepest defenders.
Backline players should not retreat automatically when pressure is strong on the ball.
Communicate attackers moving between the lines.
Protect the corridor before following wide opponents.
The nearest midfielder pressures while teammates screen likely receivers.
Deep defenders hold enough depth to attack the incoming kick.
After an intercept, use the midfield screen as the first support layer.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
The spacing between midfield and defensive lines.
Whether attackers receive uncontested between the lines.
Whether midfield pressure influences the entry.
Whether deep defenders hold intercept depth.
Whether opponent handovers are communicated.
Whether the first defensive possession connects with support.
progressions: Remove the marked central protection zone.
Add full match-like tackling.
Allow the attack to switch across the full ground width.
Introduce an immediate repeat entry after a failed exit.
Require the defensive exit to continue into a forward entry.
regressions: Allow the defence to organise before each repetition.
successIndicators: Maintain connected midfield and backline spacing.
Protect the space in front of defensive 50.
Force forward entries towards wider areas.
Intercept and connect with support before exiting.
matchApplication: A connected midfield screen reduces the pressure placed on the backline by denying easy possession at the top of defensive 50. It allows deeper defenders to hold intercept positions rather than continually following opponents towards the football.

title: Midfield Screen Sliding Gates
primarySkill: Sliding a midfield defensive screen to close central and forward passing lanes.

coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark four attacking gates across the far end: two central and two wide.
Arrange four to six defenders as a connected midfield screen.
Position attackers across the width with possession at the opposite end.
Mark left, central and right reference lanes.
Place two defensive exit gates behind the starting attacking line.
Nominate the central defender as the screen organiser.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attackers move the football laterally and attempt to pass through an attacking gate.
The defensive screen slides towards the football while protecting both central gates.
The nearest defender applies pressure and the remaining defenders close forward passing lanes.
Weak-side defenders narrow towards the corridor.
If a wide gate is used, the screen recovers inside before applying secondary pressure.
Defenders score one point for forcing a wide gate, two points for an intercept and three points for exiting after the turnover.
The coach may freeze play to assess spacing.
Teams rotate after three-minute blocks.
coachingPoints: Protect central gates before applying pressure to wide possession.
Slide while the disposal is being prepared.
Maintain eight to twelve metres between defenders.
The nearest defender closes from inside to outside.
Weak-side defenders narrow enough to protect the corridor.
Avoid having the screen become completely flat.
Communicate the direction and speed of the slide.
Recover centrally after the ball moves outside the line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the screen moves before the football arrives.
Whether central lanes remain protected.
Whether gaps open between defenders.
Whether the nearest defender separates too far from support.
Whether weak-side defenders narrow appropriately.
Whether the line recovers after wide possession.
progressions: Remove reference lanes.
Add a forward positioned behind the screen.
Introduce full tackling.
Allow long kicks over the defensive line.
Start each repetition from a turnover.
regressions: Predetermine the direction of the first two disposals.
successIndicators: Maintain suitable spacing across the line.
Force the attack into wider, less damaging areas.
matchApplication: A midfield defensive screen must move across the ground without creating central gaps. This structure reduces easy forward entries and allows teammates behind the screen to prepare for predictable wide disposals.

title: Forward-Line Press with Behind-Ball Cover
primarySkill: Applying forward-line pressure while maintaining defensive cover behind the press.
objective: Develop a forward-line defensive press that pressures the opposition’s first exit while midfield and deeper players protect space behind the pressure.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one team in a forward-half defensive structure.
Place the opposition inside defensive 50 with possession.
Mark one central and two wide exit gates near the centre line.
Position forwards around the initial possession, midfielders behind them and one or two deeper balance players.
Begin each repetition from a kick-in, intercept or defensive ground-ball win.
Nominate a forward-line pressure caller.
howTheDrillWorks:
The opposition attempts to exit defensive 50.
The nearest forward pressures the ball carrier and influences the first disposal.
Other forwards close short outlets and protect the corridor.
Midfielders compress behind the forward press and prepare to intercept the next kick.
Deeper players hold enough depth to protect a long disposal over the press.
The pressing team scores three points for regaining possession inside 50 and one point for forcing a slow wide exit.
The exiting team scores three points for a central exit and one point for a wide exit.
Reset after a successful exit, turnover or score.
coachingPoints: Pressure the first possession immediately.
Protect the central exit before chasing wide options.
Forward players must press as a connected group.
Midfielders compress behind the press rather than standing beside opponents.
Maintain a deeper balance player in case the press is broken.
Read poor kicks as intercept opportunities.
If the first line is bypassed, recover through the inside.
Show composure after regaining possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether pressure affects the first disposal.
Whether short central outlets are closed.
Whether midfielders position behind the pressure.
Whether space behind the press remains protected.
Whether forwards recover after being bypassed.
Whether regains lead to controlled scoring opportunities.
progressions: Begin from live kick-ins.
Add full match-like tackling.
Remove the marked exit gates.
Add a second opposition exit phase if the first gate is reached.
Introduce scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
regressions: Allow the press to set before play begins.
successIndicators: Pressure the opposition’s first exit possession.
Compress midfield support behind the press.
Regain possession or force a slow wide exit.
matchApplication: Forward-half pressure is effective only when the entire team supports it. The forward line applies immediate pressure, the midfield closes the next possession and deeper defenders protect against the escape over the back.

title: Three-Line Defensive Relay
primarySkill: Transferring defensive responsibility through forward, midfield and backline units.
objective: Develop coordinated defensive handovers as the football and attacking runners move through three connected defensive lines.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground, divided into three horizontal sections.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the ground into forward, midfield and defensive sections.
Position one defensive unit in each section.
Place attackers throughout all three areas.
Begin with the attacking team controlling possession in the first section.
Allow attackers to run between sections.
Nominate one communicator in each defensive line.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attack moves the football through the first defensive section.
The nearest defensive line applies pressure while the next line prepares for the likely receiver.
When an attacker crosses into another section, defenders decide whether to track or hand over.
The releasing line recovers and reconnects behind the football.
If the attack breaks one line, the next line delays while the beaten defenders recover.
Defenders score one point for forcing a backwards disposal and two points for stopping the attack in a section.
After a turnover, defenders connect through at least two lines before exiting.
Teams change roles after four-minute blocks.
coachingPoints: Communicate runners before they cross between lines.
Do not release responsibility until the next defender accepts it.
The line nearest the football pressures; the next line prepares and the deepest line balances.
Beaten players must recover behind the football.
Avoid all three lines becoming attracted to the same possession.
Preserve central protection during every handover.
Use clear names and action calls.
After winning possession, connect through the nearest support line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defensive roles are clear across the three lines.
Whether runners are handed over before becoming free.
Whether beaten defenders recover.
Whether one line becomes isolated.
Whether communication travels through the structure.
Whether the defensive exit connects through teammates.
progressions: Remove visible section boundaries.
Add full match-like tackling.
Introduce switches across the width.
Begin from rapid turnovers.
Require a full forward transition after the defensive exit.
successIndicators: Maintain pressure, cover and deeper balance.
Recover after a line is broken.
Connect the defensive exit through multiple teammates.
matchApplication: Attackers move through different parts of the ground and cannot always be followed by the same defender. Effective team defence requires responsibility to pass cleanly between forward, midfield and backline units.

title: Centre-Square Launch Defence
primarySkill: Defending opposition possession launched from the centre-square area.
objective: Develop the defensive organisation required when the opposition gains possession near the centre square and attempts to attack through the corridor at speed.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position attacking midfielders around the centre square.
Arrange defenders across midfield recovery, half-back and deep defensive roles.
Place forwards inside attacking 50.
Begin each repetition with the attacking team winning a coach-directed possession near the centre square.
Vary whether the first possession is clean, pressured or directed wide.
Rotate midfield and defensive roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team gains possession near the centre square and attacks towards goal.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier.
Other midfielders recover through the corridor and identify forward-running opponents.
Half-back defenders protect the top of defensive 50.
Deep defenders maintain goal-side positioning and prepare for the entry kick.
If outnumbered, defenders delay until support arrives.
Defenders score one point for forcing a wide entry, two points for stopping the attack and three points for exiting after the turnover.
Reset after a score, defensive exit or second turnover.
coachingPoints: Protect the corridor immediately after the centre-square possession.
The nearest player pressures without allowing an easy handball release.
Midfielders recover inside before matching wide runners.
Half-backs protect the top of defensive 50.
Deep defenders must balance opponent accountability with intercept positioning.
Delay the attack when numbers are against the defence.
Communicate runners arriving from behind.
Secure possession before beginning the rebound.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether pressure is applied to the first possession.
Whether midfielders recover centrally.
Whether half-backs protect the top of defensive 50.
Whether deep defenders remain goal-side.
Whether late runners are identified.
Whether outnumbered defenders delay effectively.
progressions: Begin from live centre-bounce contests.
Add full match-like tackling.
Introduce scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
Allow the attack to switch before entering inside 50.
Add a repeat entry after an unsuccessful exit.
regressions: Allow the defence to organise before the first possession.
successIndicators: Recover midfield numbers behind the football.
Maintain connected half-back and deep defensive lines.
Force the opposition wide, delay the attack or create a turnover.
matchApplication: A clean centre-square launch can expose the defence before normal structures are established. Players must protect the corridor, recover inside and organise the top and back of defensive 50 quickly.

title: Kick-In Lock and Re-Entry
primarySkill: Defending an opposition kick-in and creating a repeat forward entry.
objective: Develop a connected kick-in defence that protects central exits, pressures the first possession and creates opportunities for a repeat inside-50 entry.
groundSize: From the goal square to the centre square.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position the opposition for a kick-in from the goal square.
Arrange the defending team in a selected zone or hybrid structure.
Mark a central exit gate and two wide exit gates near the centre square.
Position defenders to protect short central options, wide outlets and the long contest.
Nominate a kick-in organiser.
Keep spare footballs behind the goals.
howTheDrillWorks:
The opposition begins from a kick-in.
The defending team protects the central short option and likely second possession.
The nearest defender pressures any short receiver.
Midfield defenders position for the long kick and likely spill.
If the kick-in is slow, inaccurate or directed to a stationary receiver, the defence presses.
The opposition attempts to exit through any gate.
Defenders score two points for an intercept and three points for creating a repeat inside-50 entry.
Reset after a successful exit, score or defensive regain.
coachingPoints: Protect the corridor and central short option first.
Do not allow one easy disposal to break the entire zone.
Position around the likely long-kick contest.
Pressure short receivers as possession arrives.
Weak-side players must remain connected centrally.
Recognise poor kick-ins as pressing triggers.
After an intercept, move the football quickly before the opposition resets.
Retain balance in case the attacking re-entry turns over.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the central kick-in route is protected.
Whether short receivers are pressured.
Whether defenders prepare for the second possession.
Whether the zone remains connected after a wide kick.
Whether pressing triggers are recognised.
Whether the regain creates an organised re-entry.
progressions: Remove marked exit gates.
Allow rapid play-on kick-ins.
Add full match-like contact.
Change between zone, man-on-man and hybrid structures.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios.
regressions: Restrict the opposition to a short kick.
Allow the defence to reset after each disposal.
successIndicators: Maintain zone connection through wide possession.
Regain possession and create a repeat forward entry.
matchApplication: Kick-in defence requires more than stopping the first disposal. The structure must protect the opposition’s second possession, control long contests and be ready to convert a regain into another scoring opportunity.

title: Wide Exit Funnel to Intercept
primarySkill: Funnelling opposition ball movement towards a wide intercept area.
objective: Develop a coordinated defensive structure that denies central exits, guides possession towards the boundary and prepares an intercept defender in the expected wide channel.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central attacking exit gate and two wide exit channels.
Position attackers at one end with possession.
Arrange defenders in a connected inside-out structure.
Place one intercept defender deeper in each wide channel.
Mark two rebound gates for the defence.
Begin from varied possession positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move through the central or wide exits.
The nearest defender applies inside-out pressure.
Supporting defenders close central and short options.
The defence deliberately leaves the least dangerous wide channel available.
The intercept defender reads the pressured disposal and attacks the football.
Defenders score one point for forcing the selected wide channel, two points for an intercept and three points for rebounding through a gate.
Attackers receive three points for a central exit.
Teams rotate after four-minute blocks.
coachingPoints: Deny the corridor before guiding possession wide.
Pressure must influence the disposal direction.
Do not leave multiple escape channels open.
The intercept defender should hold depth and move forward towards the kick.
Supporting defenders protect the ground-level spill.
Communicate which wide channel is being offered.
Retain cover behind the intercept attempt.
Rebound away from the original pressure where practical.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether central exits are denied.
Whether pressure directs the football predictably.
Whether defenders offer only one low-value channel.
Whether the intercept player holds suitable depth.
Whether the spill is protected.
Whether the rebound uses available space.
progressions: Remove the marked wide channels.
Allow the attack to switch before exiting.
Add full match-like tackling.
Introduce a second attacking runner in the offered channel.
Continue the rebound into a full forward entry.
successIndicators: Force possession towards a nominated wide area.
Intercept or strongly contest the wide kick.
matchApplication: A well-organised defence does not attempt to remove every option. It protects the most dangerous areas and directs the opposition towards a predictable wide disposal that can be intercepted or contested.

title: Long Down-the-Line Contest Structure
primarySkill: Organising defensive roles around a predictable long kick down the line.
objective: Develop a connected team structure around a long boundary-side contest so the defence can control the aerial ball, protect the spill and launch the next possession.
groundSize: A 70-metre boundary-side channel approximately 35 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a long channel beside the boundary.
Position an attacking kicker at one end.
Set an aerial contest 35–45 metres ahead.
Place ground-level attackers and defenders around the contest.
Position additional defenders on the old ball side who must fold behind.
Place two defensive rebound gates inside the ground.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker delivers a long kick down the line.
The aerial defender contests the football and attempts to spoil towards support.
Ground defenders protect front-and-centre, goal-side and boundary-side spill areas.
Old-side defenders fold behind the contest to provide cover and balance.
If the defence wins possession, it attempts to rebound through an inside gate.
If the attack wins the spill, play remains live towards the scoring end.
Defenders score one point for neutralising the contest and three points for winning and rebounding.
Reset with the kick delivered from a different starting angle.
coachingPoints: Pressure the kicker where possible.
Establish clear aerial, front-and-centre, goal-side and balance roles.
Avoid placing all defenders underneath the football.
Fold old-side players behind the contest.
Use the boundary to restrict attacking exits.
Direct the spoil towards teammates or safe space.
Prepare the inside rebound before possession is won.
Retain cover if the first rebound disposal turns over.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether roles are established before the kick arrives.
Whether the aerial defender gains goal-side position.
Whether ground-level spaces are protected.
Whether old-side defenders fold.
Whether the boundary limits attacking options.
Whether the defence rebounds with support.
progressions: Add a second aerial attacker.
Allow the kicker to choose short or long options.
Introduce full match-like contact.
Add a repeat contest after the first rebound.
Continue into a full transition phase.
successIndicators: Organise before the long kick arrives.
Control or neutralise the aerial contest.
Win possession and rebound through a connected option.
matchApplication: Long down-the-line kicks create predictable aerial and ground-level contests. Teams that organise roles before the ball arrives can control the spill and turn a defensive contest into an attacking transition.

title: Full-Ground Team Defence Chain
primarySkill: Maintaining connected team defence across the full length of the ground.
objective: Develop the whole team’s ability to transfer pressure, cover and balance from the forward line through midfield to the backline during continuous opposition ball movement.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position both teams in realistic full-ground structures.
Nominate defensive leaders in the forward, midfield and backline units.
Mark optional connection gates near each arc.
Begin with one team controlling possession in defensive 50.
The defending team sets a full-ground press and connected structure.
Keep spare footballs with coaches for rapid restarts.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move the football from defensive 50 to a scoring opportunity.
The defending forwards pressure the first exit.
Midfielders screen central options and support the forward press.
The backline maintains depth and tracks attacking movement ahead of the football.
If one defensive line is broken, the next line delays while teammates recover.
After winning possession, the defending team transitions through the nearest connection gate.
If the exit fails, teams immediately return to defensive roles.
Play continues for two-to-three-minute blocks before coaching review.
coachingPoints: Maintain connection between all three defensive units.
The ball-side line pressures while the next line prepares.
Protect the corridor throughout the ground.
Compress when pressure is strong and protect behind when it is weak.
Communicate runners moving between lines.
Recover after being bypassed.
Retain one balance layer behind aggressive pressure.
After winning possession, spread without abandoning turnover protection.
Reset immediately if the rebound fails.
Avoid having the team split into isolated groups.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
The spacing between forward, midfield and defensive lines.
Whether the corridor remains protected.
Whether pressure transfers between units.
Whether broken lines recover.
Whether deep cover remains behind the football.
Whether the team spreads effectively after a turnover.
Whether defensive shape is restored after a failed rebound.
progressions: Use full match-like contact.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
Allow unrestricted kick-ins and stoppages.
Introduce immediate repeat entries after failed exits.
Remove all coach-directed resets.
regressions: Limit the attack to one side.
Pause after each line is broken.
Reduce player numbers and use neutral support players.
successIndicators: Recover after defensive lines are broken.
Win possession and transition without losing balance.
matchApplication: Team defence is a full-ground responsibility. Forward pressure, midfield screening and backline positioning must operate as one connected system rather than as separate units.

title: Structured Team Defence Assessment
primarySkill: Applying connected team-defence structures across multiple field positions.
objective: Assess whether players can independently apply the structured team-defence principles introduced through TD-061 to TD-069 during realistic, continuous game scenarios.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two-thirds or the full ground.
Arrange both teams in realistic positional structures.
Prepare the following starting scenarios:
Opposition possession across half-forward
Midfield screen under lateral ball movement
Forward-line defensive press
Centre-square attacking launch
Opposition kick-in
Long kick down the line
Full-ground transition
Assign coaches to observe each defensive unit.
Rotate teams after completing all scenarios.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each repetition from one prepared scenario.
The attacking team attempts to move the football and score without disposal restrictions.
The defence must organise the appropriate structure independently.
Forward, midfield and backline units must remain connected.
Defensive responsibilities are handed over as players move between lines.
After winning possession, the defence attempts a controlled transition.
Failed exits produce an immediate repeat attacking phase.
Each repetition lasts 60–120 seconds before the next scenario begins.
coachingPoints: Connect midfield and backline spacing.
Slide defensive screens with the football.
Support forward pressure with midfield compression and deeper cover.
Transfer runners and responsibility between lines.
Protect the corridor during centre-square launches.
Defend kick-ins beyond the first disposal.
Funnel possession towards predictable wide contests.
Organise aerial and ground-level roles around long kicks.
Maintain full-ground connection.
Transition with support while retaining balance behind the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defensive units maintain connected spacing.
Whether midfield screens protect central space.
Whether forward pressure receives support from behind.
Whether runners are handed over clearly.
Whether centre-square attacks are delayed or forced wide.
Whether kick-in structures protect the second possession.
Whether wide funnels create predictable contests.
Whether long-kick spill roles are organised.
Whether the entire team shifts together.
Whether defensive wins lead to composed transitions.
Whether failed exits trigger an immediate reset.
progressions: Remove all advance notice of the starting scenario.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure consequences.
Allow the attacking team to select its preferred method of breaking the defence.
Continue every defensive regain into a complete attacking phase.
Use uninterrupted match simulation with coach scoring only.
regressions: Assess one structural principle at a time.
Allow defensive leaders to set the structure before each restart.
successIndicators: Connect forward, midfield and defensive units.
Slide and compress in response to ball movement.
Support pressure with cover and balance.
Apply the required structure without constant coach direction.
matchApplication: This assessment tests whether the team can apply connected defensive structures across the full range of common Australian football situations. It measures the relationship between forward pressure, midfield screening, backline positioning, intercept creation and defensive transition.

title: No-Pressure Defensive Drop
primarySkill: Dropping defensive lines when the opposition ball carrier has uncontested time and space.
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise the absence of pressure on the football and collectively protect deeper space before the opposition can kick over the defensive structure.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Arrange the defending team in a high, middle and deep line.
Position attackers across the full width and at different depths.
Place three target zones behind the deepest defensive line.
Begin with an attacking ball carrier 40–50 metres from the target zones.
At selected repetitions, the ball carrier begins under pressure; at others, the player begins completely free.
Nominate the deepest defender as the primary drop communicator.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move the football into one of the target zones.
When the ball carrier is under pressure, the defence may hold or compress its shape.
When the ball carrier has uncontested time, the deepest defender calls “drop”.
All defensive lines adjust backwards while maintaining connection.
The defence protects the space behind first, then closes the receiver as the football travels.
Defenders score one point for preventing possession behind the line and two points for an intercept.
After winning possession, defenders exit through either wide gate.
Reset with a different level of pressure on the starting ball carrier.
coachingPoints: Recognise whether genuine pressure exists on the football.
Drop before the kick is released, not after it travels overhead.
Maintain connected spacing while moving backwards.
Avoid turning completely away from the football.
Deep defenders must communicate early and clearly.
Protect the corridor and deepest dangerous target.
Close the receiver while the football is travelling.
Step forward again when pressure is restored.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players correctly identify the absence of pressure.
Whether the drop begins before the kick.
Whether all defensive lines adjust together.
Whether gaps appear during the retreat.
Whether defenders retain vision of opponents and the football.
Whether the group steps forward when pressure returns.
progressions: Remove the coach-directed pressure variations.
Allow attackers to run and carry before kicking.
Add full match-like tackling.
Introduce a second attacking wave after the first kick.
Require the defence to rebound through the corridor after an intercept.
successIndicators: Recognise when the football is not pressured.
Drop before the attacking kick is released.
matchApplication: When an opposition player has time and space, a high defensive line is vulnerable to a kick over the back. The team must recognise this early, protect deeper space and then close the next receiver as the football travels.

title: Backward Possession Compression Chain
primarySkill: Compressing the defensive structure after consecutive opposition disposals move backwards.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to use repeated backwards opposition possession as a signal to move forward, reduce available space and build coordinated pressure.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position the attacking team across three horizontal bands.
Arrange the defence in connected forward, midfield and deeper lines.
Place three attacking exit gates behind the deepest defensive line.
Begin with the attack holding possession in the middle band.
Encourage attackers to use backwards possession when forward options are blocked.
Nominate one defender in each line to communicate compression.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to progress through an exit gate.
The defence initially protects space and applies controlled pressure.
After one backwards disposal, the nearest line steps forward.
After a second consecutive backwards disposal, all defensive lines compress aggressively.
Defenders close the next short options while retaining balance behind the press.
Attackers may attempt to break the pressure with a forward kick or switch.
Defenders score three points for a turnover following consecutive backwards disposals.
After winning possession, defenders rebound through either side gate.
coachingPoints: Treat backwards possession as a reduction in attacking threat.
Step while the backwards disposal is travelling.
Maintain connected spacing between lines.
The nearest defender closes the receiver’s forward side.
Supporting defenders remove short and central options.
Retain one deeper balance player.
Do not press if the backwards receiver has clear time to kick over the structure.
Recover immediately if the compression is broken.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the team recognises consecutive backwards possession.
Whether each defensive line steps together.
Whether the next receiver is pressured.
Whether short exit options are removed.
Whether balance remains behind the press.
Whether the defence recovers after a successful forward break.
progressions: Remove the requirement for consecutive backwards disposals.
Add full match-like tackling.
Allow rapid switches during the compression.
Reduce the playing area.
Continue the defensive regain into a forward entry.
regressions: The coach calls the compression trigger.
Require three backwards disposals before the press.
successIndicators: Recognise backwards possession as a compression opportunity.
Move forward while the football travels.
Create a turnover or force a hurried long disposal.
matchApplication: Teams can reclaim territory when the opposition is forced backwards. Coordinated compression reduces the opponent’s available space and can turn harmless retreating possession into a turnover opportunity.

title: Match-Up to Zone Release
primarySkill: Transitioning from direct opponent accountability into space-based zone defence.
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when direct match-ups should be released and replaced by a connected zone structure during slower opposition possession.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Begin with each defender assigned a direct opponent.
Position both teams across two-thirds of the ground.
Place three attacking gates at one end.
Explain the zone-release triggers:
Opposition mark with no immediate play-on
Backwards kick
Possession moved outside the dangerous corridor
All defenders recovered behind the football
Nominate a defensive leader who may call “zone”.
Mark reference zone positions initially.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move through a scoring gate.
The defence begins in direct match-ups.
When an approved trigger occurs, the defensive leader calls “zone”.
Defenders release less dangerous wide opponents and occupy assigned space.
Players protect the corridor, short central options and space behind the structure.
If the attack plays on quickly or breaks the zone, defenders re-establish direct accountability.
Defenders score one point for completing the tactical transition and two points for an intercept.
After a turnover, the defence exits through either wide gate.
coachingPoints: Do not release a dangerous opponent without communication.
Transition only when the football and defensive numbers permit.
Protect central space before moving to the wider zone positions.
Clearly identify which players remain directly accountable.
Use names and calls during every handover.
Continue scanning opponents after releasing them.
Return to direct responsibility if the zone is broken.
Maintain pressure on the football during the tactical change.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the correct trigger is recognised.
Whether the zone call is early and clear.
Whether dangerous opponents remain covered.
Whether defenders move to useful space rather than empty grass.
Whether the corridor is protected.
Whether direct accountability is restored after the zone is broken.
progressions: Remove visible zone references.
Allow the attacking team to disguise tempo changes.
Add full match-like tackling.
Permit multiple tactical transitions within one phase.
Let players call the change without a nominated leader.
regressions: The coach calls the zone transition.
successIndicators: Release opponents only after clear communication.
Return to direct defence when required.
matchApplication: Teams may begin with direct match-ups but shift into a zone when the opposition slows play or moves into less dangerous areas. The transition must occur collectively or free opponents will appear between structures.

title: Fat-Side Diagonal Switch Defence
primarySkill: Defending a long diagonal switch into open space on the far side of the ground.
objective: Develop the positioning and movement required to protect the far side of the ground against a long diagonal switch while maintaining central defensive connection.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground using full width.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position the attacking team with possession near one boundary.
Place attackers across the corridor and far-side wing.
Arrange defenders in connected ball-side and weak-side positions.
Place a target gate in the far-side channel and two others centrally.
Nominate one attacking player as a possible diagonal switch receiver.
Position defensive support around the expected far-side contest.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attack circulates possession on the ball side.
The far-side attacker moves into space for a diagonal kick.
Weak-side defenders narrow centrally while remaining able to reach the switch receiver.
When the diagonal switch is prepared, the nearest weak-side defender closes the receiver.
Supporting defenders move to the likely aerial and ground-level contest.
Ball-side defenders recover through central positions behind the football.
Defenders score one point for forcing a contest and two points for winning the switch possession.
After a turnover, defenders rebound through the opposite side gate.
coachingPoints: Weak-side defenders must not stand on the far boundary.
Maintain a position that protects the corridor and allows access to the switch.
Read the kicker’s body position and available kicking lane.
Move while the diagonal kick is being prepared.
Arrive goal-side of the far-side receiver.
Organise aerial, front-and-centre and deeper support.
Old ball-side defenders recover through central space.
Avoid overcommitting so early that the attack can use the corridor.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether weak-side defenders begin centrally.
Whether the long switch is recognised before release.
Whether the receiver is contested on arrival.
Whether ground-level support is organised.
Whether old ball-side defenders recover centrally.
Whether the corridor remains protected during the shift.
progressions: Allow the attack to fake the diagonal and use the corridor.
Add full match-like contact.
Introduce two possible far-side receivers.
Begin from an unpredictable turnover.
Continue the defensive win into a full-ground transition.
regressions: Mark starting positions for weak-side defenders.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor while covering the far side.
Organise support around the expected spill.
Recover the old ball side behind the football.
matchApplication: Long diagonal switches can expose a defensive structure concentrated on one side. Weak-side players must remain connected centrally while positioning close enough to contest the far-side receiver.

title: Space Behind the Press Protection
primarySkill: Protecting the space behind an aggressive high defensive press.
objective: Develop the deeper cover required behind a forward or midfield press so one long disposal cannot completely break the defensive structure.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position the defending team in an aggressive forward and midfield press.
Place one or two deeper defenders behind the main defensive structure.
Position attacking targets in three deep channels.
Begin with the attack attempting to exit from defensive 50.
Allow attackers to use short possession or a long kick over the press.
Nominate a deep defensive organiser.
howTheDrillWorks:
The forward and midfield defenders pressure the attacking exit.
Deeper defenders adjust according to pressure on the ball carrier.
When pressure is strong, deep defenders may move higher and compress.
When pressure is weak, they hold or increase depth.
If the attack kicks over the press, the deep defenders contest, intercept or delay.
Beaten pressing players recover through central routes.
Defenders score one point for neutralising the long kick and two points for winning and exiting.
Reset after a successful attacking exit, turnover or defensive rebound.
coachingPoints: Aggressive pressure must always have protection behind it.
Deep defenders must read the quality of pressure on the football.
Hold enough depth to move forward towards the long kick.
Communicate opponents moving behind the press.
Do not stand directly beside the deepest attacker.
Recovering players must sprint through the corridor.
If the long kick is won, use supporting players rather than immediately returning the football to pressure.
Reconnect the entire defensive structure after the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether a deeper defender remains behind the press.
Whether depth changes according to pressure.
Whether long targets are communicated.
Whether the deepest kick is contested moving forward.
Whether beaten press players recover centrally.
Whether the defensive rebound uses support.
progressions: Add multiple deep attacking targets.
Remove the nominated deep organiser.
Add full match-like contact.
Allow the attack to switch before kicking long.
Continue play through a second contest after the long kick.
regressions: Allow the coach to call the required depth.
successIndicators: Adjust depth according to ball pressure.
Contest long disposals over the press.
Recover beaten players behind the football.
matchApplication: High defensive pressure can create turnovers but also exposes space behind the team. Effective structures retain deeper cover that can intercept, contest or delay if the opposition escapes with a long kick.

title: Defensive Numbers Without Overcollapse
primarySkill: Bringing defensive numbers towards the football while retaining outside and deeper protection.
objective: Develop players’ ability to support the immediate defensive contest without having the entire team collapse into congestion and expose outside space.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central contest zone and four outside exit gates.
Begin with equal numbers around a loose football inside the contest zone.
Position additional defenders outside as release-lane and balance players.
The attacking team attempts to win the contest and exit through any gate.
Defenders decide how many players are required inside the contest.
Rotate inside and outside roles after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a loose or contested football.
The nearest defenders pressure the immediate possession.
Additional defenders move closer but stop in likely release lanes.
One defender remains goal-side and another protects the weak side.
If the football exits congestion, outside defenders become the next pressure line.
Defenders score one point for denying the first release and two points for a turnover.
Attackers score double points if they escape through an unattended outside gate.
After winning possession, defenders rebound through the safest available gate.
coachingPoints: Bring enough numbers to affect the contest, not every available player.
Identify pressure, inside cover, outside release and deeper balance roles.
Protect the first clean handball away from congestion.
Weak-side defenders should narrow without entering the contest.
Maintain one player behind the football.
Communicate when no additional defender is required.
If the attack escapes, rotate pressure rather than chasing from behind.
Spread immediately after winning possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:

title: Half-Forward Arc Pressing Trap

Retain deeper cover behind the press.
Nominate a trapping side before the first block.
howTheDrillWorks:
The opposition attempts to exit the defensive half.
The nearest forward closes from the corridor side and directs possession towards the nominated boundary.
Supporting forwards remove the inside handball and short central kick.
Midfielders compress into the next likely possession.
Deeper defenders protect the long kick over the trap.
The pressing team scores one point for forcing possession along the boundary and three points for a turnover.
The exiting team scores three points for a corridor break and one point for a wide exit.
After a regain, the pressing team attacks goal with unrestricted football.
coachingPoints: Establish the trapping direction before pressure arrives.
The first defender must close from inside to outside.
Supporting players protect the return disposal into the corridor.
Midfielders compress behind the first pressure line.
Retain deep cover against the long release.
Do not chase a backwards disposal that improves the opposition’s angle.
Recognise when the trap has failed and recover goal-side.
Use composure after the regain.

Whether pressure directs possession towards the nominated side.
Whether the corridor return is protected.
Whether midfielders close the second possession.
Whether deep cover remains behind the trap.

Whether the regain creates a controlled scoring opportunity.

Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.

title: Defensive Reset After Opposition Switch Mark
primarySkill: Rebuilding defensive shape during the pause created by an opposition switch mark.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to use an opposition switch mark to reorganise, recover central connection and prepare for the next disposal before play resumes.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground using full width.

Begin with possession on one wing.
Arrange the defence in a ball-side shape with weak-side cover.
The attack completes a long switch to a player who takes a mark.
Defenders begin in deliberately varied positions.
Place three attacking target gates behind the defensive structure.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attack completes the nominated switch and takes a mark.
The nearest defender sets the mark.
All other defenders use the pause to recover through central positions.
Players identify new opponents, protect the corridor and restore line spacing.
When the marked player moves or plays on, the new ball-side defender applies pressure.
The attack attempts to move through a target gate.

coachingPoints: Use the marked-ball pause as active organisation time.

title: Live Defensive System Selection

objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise match cues and collectively select between direct accountability, zone protection, aggressive press and controlled delay.

Late-game lead protection

All defenders organise into the selected structure.
Players may change system if the situation changes.

After each repetition, the group briefly identifies why the system was chosen before restarting.
coachingPoints: System choice must reflect pressure, numbers, field position and score context.

After winning possession, the team must transition while retaining turnover protection.

coachingPoints: Drop when the football is unpressured and space behind is threatened.
Compress collectively after opposition backwards possession.
Transition between match-up and zone structures with clear communication.
Protect the corridor while defending long switches.
Retain cover behind aggressive pressure.

Select suitable systems without coach direction.
Transition after defensive wins without losing balance.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the structured and adaptable team-defence behaviours required in advanced Australian football. It measures whether the team can read changing conditions, select the correct defensive response and remain connected from the forward line to the deepest defender.

title: Late-Game Lead Protection Structure
primarySkill: Protecting a narrow scoreboard lead through controlled defensive structure.
objective: Develop players’ ability to defend a narrow lead by protecting high-value central space, forcing predictable wide possession and avoiding unnecessary defensive risks.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback

Begin with three minutes remaining.
Position the attacking team in possession near half-back or the centre square.
Arrange the defence in connected forward, midfield and backline units.

Nominate defensive leaders responsible for time, score and structural communication.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to score enough points to take the lead.
The defence protects the corridor, central forward-entry lanes and space behind the deepest line.

matchApplication: Protecting a narrow lead requires different decisions from normal open play. The team must retain enough pressure to prevent easy progression while reducing the risk of turnovers, corridor exposure and one disposal breaking the entire defensive structure.

title: Must-Regain Full-Ground Press

coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback

Begin with the opposition taking a kick-in or holding possession in defensive 50.
Assign direct opponents across the ground.
