Mark one central and two wide opposition exit gates.
Nominate one pressure caller in each line.
Position a coach near the scoreboard to update time.
howTheDrillWorks:
The opposition attempts to retain possession and run down the clock.
The pressing team applies close accountability and aggressive pressure.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier while teammates deny short uncontested options.
Players behind the press step forward to reduce usable space.
The team may leave a low-value long contest available while removing easy possession.
After regaining the football, the pressing team attacks goal immediately but with organised support.
If the opposition exits through a gate, the press must recover and re-establish further up the ground.
The repetition ends when time expires, the pressing team levels the score or the opposition retains possession for 40 seconds.

Maintain direct accountability on short options.
Pressure the ball carrier’s preferred side.
Compress every line behind the first pressure action.

title: Defensive Overload Spare Identification

Protect the corridor and players closest to goal.

title: Isolated Key Forward Peel-Off Defence

matchApplication: Key forwards are often isolated to prevent defensive support. Successful team defence depends on the direct contest, pressure on the kick and well-timed assistance that does not create an uncontested opponent elsewhere.

title: Fast Centre-Launch Emergency Defence

title: Kick-In Chain Interruption

title: Final-Ninety-Seconds Boundary Defence

Run repeated scenarios from marks, throw-ins, ground balls and free kicks.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to score before time expires.
The defence protects the inside route and directs possession towards the boundary.
At boundary stoppages, defenders protect the corridor-side exit.
If the defence wins possession, players decide whether to retain, advance along the boundary or take a safe mark.
If the football leaves the area, the coach restarts with the appropriate scenario and adjusts the clock.
Deliberate illegal time wasting results in a turnover or free kick to the attack.
The attacking team receives an immediate repeat entry after a rushed central defensive turnover.
The repetition ends when time expires, the score changes or the defence establishes secure possession.
coachingPoints: Know the score and remaining time.
Protect the corridor side of every boundary contest.
Use the boundary without relying on illegal or reckless actions.
Maintain one defender behind the immediate contest.
Prevent the attacking team from releasing backwards into central space.
Communicate stoppage roles before the restart.
After winning possession, select a legal low-risk option.
Avoid taking the football into unnecessary central congestion.
Remain prepared for the opposition to switch quickly.
Do not concede avoidable free kicks through undisciplined contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players understand the match situation.
Whether the inside stoppage exit is protected.
Whether a deeper balance player remains.
Whether contact remains legal.
Whether the defence uses the boundary intelligently.
Whether players communicate restart roles.
Whether possession decisions suit the clock.
Whether the team remains alert to a switch.
Whether the defence avoids unnecessary free kicks.
progressions: Reduce the lead to one point.
Begin with 45 seconds remaining.
Start from a defensive free kick near the boundary.

Prevent a high-value central scoring opportunity.
preserve the lead until time expires.
matchApplication: The final stages of close matches demand precise tactical and legal decision making. Boundary control, stoppage organisation and possession security can prevent the opposition from gaining the central access required for a winning score.

title: Player-Led Defensive Command Chain
primarySkill: Organising and adapting team defence through player-led communication.
objective: Develop players’ ability to lead the defensive structure, communicate tactical changes and solve emerging match problems without direct coach instruction.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Arrange both teams in realistic structures.
Nominate one leader in the forward line, midfield and backline.
Give only the attacking team the initial scenario information.
Possible attacking plans include:
Repeated switches
Corridor handball chain
Long down-the-line exit
Isolated key forward
Possession retention
Numerical overload
The coach remains silent during each playing phase.
Defensive leaders may call “match”, “zone”, “press”, “drop”, “delay” or “release”.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins using its selected plan.
Defensive players identify the attacking method through live play.
Unit leaders communicate information through the forward, midfield and backline.
A defensive system is selected and applied.
Leaders may change the structure as the attacking method evolves.
Players outside formal leadership roles contribute local information and confirm responsibilities.
After winning possession, the defence transitions while retaining turnover protection.
The coach reviews the communication and decisions only after the phase ends.
coachingPoints: Leaders must communicate what is happening, not merely demand greater effort.
Calls should include the problem, system and immediate action.
Information must travel through every line.
The deepest players communicate space and opponents behind the structure.
The nearest players communicate pressure and immediate options.
Confirm responsibility after every tactical change.
Avoid conflicting calls from several leaders.
Change the system when the original solution is no longer suitable.
Non-leaders must acknowledge and support instructions.
Maintain calm, specific communication during high-pressure phases.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players recognise the attacking method.
Whether leaders communicate early.
Whether calls are specific and actionable.
Whether information reaches all defensive lines.
Whether teammates acknowledge instructions.
Whether the selected defensive system suits the problem.
Whether leaders change the structure when required.
Whether local communication supports the broader system.
Whether conflicting calls are resolved.
Whether the team remains organised without coach intervention.
progressions: Remove nominated leaders.
Change the attacking plan during the phase.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure information.
Use full match-like contact.

title: Advanced Tactical Team Defence Assessment
primarySkill: Applying advanced team-defence solutions to changing scoreboard, structural and numerical problems.
objective: Assess whether players can independently select, communicate and execute advanced defensive responses across complex match scenarios.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Arrange both teams in realistic full-ground structures.
Nominate player leaders but do not provide them with every scenario in advance.
Prepare the following scenarios:
Defending a four-point lead
Needing an immediate possession regain
Defending an attacking numerical overload
Supporting an isolated key defender
Emergency defence after a clean centre launch
Disrupting a rehearsed kick-in chain
Maintaining a press through opposition switches
Defending a boundary stoppage in the final 90 seconds
Player-led system selection
Assign coaches to observe structural, technical, communication and decision-making outcomes.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each repetition from one prepared scenario.
The scoreboard, time and player numbers are announced only when relevant.
The attacking team attempts to exploit the specific tactical problem.
The defence must identify the situation and select an appropriate response.
Players organise pressure, cover, balance, accountability and depth.
Tactical systems may change during the repetition.
After winning possession, the defence must make an exit or attacking decision suited to the scoreboard.
Each phase lasts 60–150 seconds before the next scenario begins.
coachingPoints: Adjust defensive risk according to score and time.
Protect the corridor and highest-value scoring space.
Close short options when immediate possession regain is required.
Delay and prioritise danger when outnumbered.
Support isolated defenders only when released opponents are covered.
React immediately to clean centre launches.
Defend kick-in chains beyond the first possession.
Shift efficiently through opposition switches.
Use boundary and stoppage structures legally.
Communicate tactical changes through every line.
Allow player leaders to solve problems without waiting for the coach.
Retain balance after defensive regains and attacking transitions.

Whether the chosen level of defensive risk is appropriate.
Whether central and high-value space remains protected.
Whether pressing structures retain support behind.

Whether kick-in chains are interrupted.

Continue through uninterrupted match simulation.
Remove nominated defensive leaders.
Require players to review and grade their own defensive decisions after each block.

Provide the defence with the scenario before the restart.
Allow a brief player huddle before each phase.
successIndicators: Adjust risk according to scoreboard and time.
Maintain pressure, cover, balance and depth.
Support isolated contests without creating free opponents.

matchApplication: This assessment combines advanced scoreboard, structural, numerical and leadership challenges. It measures whether the team can recognise complex match problems, select the correct defensive response and execute it collectively under realistic pressure.

title: Small-Forward Ground-Level Containment
primarySkill: Containing dangerous small forwards around inside-50 marking contests.
objective: Develop a coordinated defensive structure that prevents opposition small forwards from winning clean ground-level possession and creating immediate scoring opportunities.
groundSize: Inside defensive 50, using approximately 45 metres × 40 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position one attacking and one defending tall player in a marking contest.
Place two attacking small forwards around the anticipated ground-ball area.
Position three ground-level defenders in front-and-centre, goal-side and outside-balance roles.
Add an attacking feeder outside 50 and one defensive pressure player near the feeder.
Place two wide defensive exit gates.
Rotate aerial, small-forward, ground-defence and feeder roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking feeder delivers the football towards the tall marking contest.
The aerial defender attempts to mark or spoil towards defensive support.
Ground defenders establish front-and-centre, goal-side and outside-balance positions while the football is travelling.
If an attacking small forward wins the spill, the nearest defender applies immediate pressure.
The second defender closes the most likely handball or snap-release lane.
The third defender protects the goal side and remains available for a second spill.
If the defence wins possession, players must secure the football and exit through a wide gate.
The attack scores for a goal or controlled central possession; the defence scores for a neutralised crumb, turnover or successful exit.
coachingPoints: Organise ground-level roles before the aerial contest occurs.
Protect front-and-centre space without standing directly underneath the football.
Maintain goal-side position on the most dangerous small forward.
The nearest defender pressures the crumb winner while teammates close releases.
Avoid having every defender attack the same ground ball.
Communicate changes in small-forward positioning.
Expect second and third spills rather than assuming the first contest ends the phase.
Use legal body positioning to deny the direct route to goal.
If clean possession is unavailable, create a stoppage or knock the football towards support.
Exit with width rather than returning possession directly into congestion.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defensive ground roles are established while the kick travels.
Whether attacking small forwards gain inside position.
Whether the first crumb possession receives immediate pressure.
Whether defenders protect handball and snap-release lanes.
Whether one defender remains behind the contest.
Whether defenders continue through multiple spills.
Whether the exit is secure and supported.
progressions: Add a third attacking small forward.
Introduce full match-like contact.
Allow the feeder to vary entry height and direction.
Add a repeat entry after an incomplete exit.
Begin with the attacking small forwards changing positions before the entry.
Continue a successful defensive exit into full-ground transition.
regressions: Allow defenders to set their ground positions before the kick.
Use controlled touch pressure on the crumb winner.
successIndicators: Establish ground-level defensive roles before the contest.
Remain goal-side of dangerous small forwards.
Protect the immediate release and scoring lanes.
Win, neutralise or force the football away from goal.
matchApplication: Inside defensive 50, a successful spoil can still result in a goal if attacking small forwards control the ground ball. This drill develops the team structure required to defend both the aerial contest and the dangerous possession that follows.

title: Twin Tall Forward Rotation Defence
primarySkill: Coordinating defensive responsibility against two tall forwards using changing leading patterns.
objective: Develop the communication and rotation required to defend two tall forwards without allowing crossing leads, deep isolation or defensive assistance to create an uncontested target.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position two tall forwards and two direct defenders inside attacking 50.
Add one defensive support player and two ground-level players for each team.
Position two attacking feeders across half-forward.
The tall forwards may lead high, deep, laterally or cross each other.
Place two wide defensive exit gates.
Rotate tall-forward, key-defender, support and ground-level roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking feeders move the football across half-forward.
The two tall forwards create coordinated leading patterns.
Direct defenders communicate whether to stay, switch or pass responsibility.
The support defender may peel towards the more dangerous contest only when the released opponent is covered.
Ground defenders protect front-and-centre and goal-side spill areas.
The attack attempts to mark or gain controlled possession inside the scoring zone.
If the defence wins possession, it exits through a wide gate.
The defence scores for forcing a wide entry, neutralising both tall targets and completing an exit.
coachingPoints: Maintain goal-side body position on both tall forwards.
Communicate crossing leads before the forwards separate.
Protect the deeper and more dangerous lead first.
Do not switch automatically; assess whether staying preserves better position.
The support defender must confirm coverage before peeling off.
Pressure on the entry kick determines how aggressively defenders can hold position.
Avoid both key defenders following the same leading forward.
Maintain ground-level structure around the likely contest.
Reassign opponents immediately after a spoil or turnover.
Use width and support after the defensive win.

Allow the coach to call switch-or-stay decisions.

Make appropriate stay, switch and peel decisions.
Neutralise the entry or force it towards a low-value area.
matchApplication: Teams often use two tall forwards to create crossing leads, isolate a preferred match-up or prevent intercept support. Defenders must coordinate responsibility across both threats rather than treating each contest independently.

title: Defensive Wing Fold and Corridor Screen
primarySkill: Using the defensive-side wing to fold behind possession and protect the corridor.
objective: Develop the defensive wing’s ability to narrow behind the football, screen central movement, support long contests and expand again when possession changes sides.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground using the full width.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position the attacking team with possession on one wing.
Arrange defenders across forward, midfield and backline units.
Nominate one defender on the opposite wing as the defensive folding wing.
Place attacking gates through the corridor and both wings.
Establish a likely long-kick contest on the ball side.
Place two defensive rebound gates on the opposite side.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attack moves possession along one side of the ground.
The defensive-side wing narrows behind the football into a corridor-screening position.
If the attack kicks long down the line, the wing folds behind the contest to provide cover or ground-level support.
If the attack switches, the wing expands towards the new receiver while another teammate assumes the central screen.
The wing communicates runners entering from behind.
Defenders score one point for denying the corridor, two points for winning the long contest and three points for rebounding through the opposite gate.

Rotate wing and midfield roles after each block.

title: Half-Back Intercept-to-Outlet Unit
primarySkill: Connecting half-back intercept positioning with a reliable first outlet.

Place one defensive midfielder in front of the half-back line.
Position two outlet players towards the wings.
Mark one central and two wide outlet gates.
Begin each repetition with the attack controlling possession across half-forward.

title: Midfield Stoppage Sweep and Cover
primarySkill: Positioning a defensive midfielder behind a stoppage to protect the opposition’s forward exit.

title: High-Forward Exit Denial Rotation

title: Wet-Weather Territory Defence

title: Four-Phase Team Defence Match Rehearsal
primarySkill: Maintaining the team defensive game plan through four consecutive match phases.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to move between major defensive phases without losing structure, communication or tactical clarity.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Arrange both teams in full positional structures.
Establish four consecutive phases:
Opposition kick-in
Midfield stoppage
Turnover transition
Repeat inside-50 entry
Nominate defensive leaders in each unit.
The coach controls restarts but provides no tactical instruction during play.
Set a scoreboard and time situation appropriate to the playing group.
Assign assistant coaches to observe separate defensive units.
howTheDrillWorks:
Phase One: The opposition begins with a kick-in and attempts to exit defensive 50.
When the phase ends, the coach immediately starts Phase Two from a midfield stoppage.
After the stoppage possession is resolved, the coach creates Phase Three through an unpredictable turnover.
The teams transition at full speed and play until a forward entry or defensive stop occurs.
The coach then introduces Phase Four as an immediate repeat entry against the defending team.
The defence must reorganise between phases without a huddle or coach instruction.
A successful defensive stop must be followed by an exit suited to the score and pressure.
Complete four to six full sequences before changing the scoreboard or tactical condition.
coachingPoints: Carry defensive communication from one phase into the next.
Defend kick-in possession beyond the first disposal.
Establish pressure, cover and balance around the stoppage.
React immediately when possession changes.
Protect the corridor during open transition.
Reassign opponents rather than searching for original match-ups.
Reset shape immediately after unsuccessful exits.
Maintain pressure and ground-level organisation during repeat entries.
Adjust risk according to score and time.
Retain turnover protection after defensive wins.
Leaders should organise while players are moving.
Complete every phase rather than mentally resetting early.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether kick-in defence protects the second possession.
Whether the midfield stoppage has clear pressure and sweep roles.
Whether turnover reaction is immediate.
Whether the corridor is protected during transition.
Whether opponents are reassigned quickly.
Whether defensive lines reconnect before the repeat entry.
Whether ground-level and aerial contest roles are organised.
Whether player leaders communicate between phases.
Whether fatigue causes structural errors.
Whether defensive exits suit the match situation.
progressions: Remove advance notice of the phase order.
Change scoreboard information during the sequence.
Allow the attacking team to select its kick-in and stoppage methods.
Reduce recovery between sequences.
Remove nominated defensive leaders.
Continue all regains into complete attacking phases.
regressions: Rehearse two phases at a time.
Allow 10 seconds for defensive organisation between phases.
Announce each phase before the restart.
Permit one short player huddle per sequence.
successIndicators: Maintain defensive connection through all four phases.
Defend kick-ins and stoppages with clear roles.
Win possession and make an appropriate transition decision.
matchApplication: Matches move rapidly between set plays, turnovers, open transition and repeat entries. This rehearsal tests whether the team’s defensive game plan remains stable when those phases occur consecutively without coaching pauses.

title: Team Defence Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Applying the complete team-defence system in unrestricted match conditions.
objective: Assess whether the team can independently establish, maintain and adapt a complete defensive system across all major Australian football phases and match situations.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Arrange both teams in full match structures.
Nominate defensive leaders, but require all players to communicate local information.
Prepare a balanced assessment sequence containing:
Slow opposition possession
Fast centre-square launch
Opposition kick-in
Forward-half press
Long down-the-line contest
Full-width switch
Outnumbered defensive transition
Repeat inside-50 entries
Boundary stoppage
Late-game lead protection
Immediate possession-regain requirement
Opposition-specific attacking pattern
Assign coaches to assess forward, midfield, backline and full-team behaviours.
Use a scoring rubric for structure, communication, pressure, contest work, adaptability and transition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each scenario without prescribing the required defensive solution.
The attacking team attempts to exploit the starting condition using unrestricted football.
The defence identifies the problem, selects a system and organises responsibilities.
Play continues through disposals, contests, turnovers and transitions until a score, controlled exit or natural stoppage occurs.
Tactical conditions may change during a repetition.
After a defensive win, the team must select an exit or attacking transition appropriate to the scoreboard and pressure.
Failed exits result in immediate repeat entries.
Coaches record outcomes without interrupting normal play.
Players complete a brief self-assessment between major blocks.
The final phase is an uninterrupted match-simulation block in which the defence must operate without coach instruction.
coachingPoints: Establish connected defensive shape before applying unnecessary pressure.
Maintain goal-side positioning and protect high-value central space.
Coordinate pressure, cover and balance around possession.
Adjust defensive depth according to pressure on the football.
Communicate opponent handovers and movement between lines.
Protect the corridor while maintaining weak-side coverage.
Use pressing triggers collectively.
Delay correctly when outnumbered.
Organise aerial, ground-level and stoppage contests.
Create intercept opportunities through influenced disposals.
Reset immediately after unsuccessful exits and repeat entries.
Select between direct accountability, zone, press and delay according to the situation.
Adjust risk to scoreboard and time.
Retain turnover protection after winning possession.
Use player leadership to organise the system.
Maintain legal technique and structural discipline under fatigue.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
The speed and accuracy of initial defensive organisation.
Connection between forward, midfield and backline units.
Goal-side positioning and corridor protection.
Pressure, cover and balance around the football.
Defensive depth relative to ball pressure.
Weak-side and behind-ball coverage.
Opponent handovers and runner communication.
Recognition of pressing triggers.
Delay decisions when outnumbered.
Aerial, ground-level and stoppage organisation.
Repeat defensive efforts and reset speed.
Tactical system selection and changes.
Scoreboard and time awareness.
Leadership and player-led problem solving.
Contact safety and discipline.
Quality of the first possession after a defensive win.
Turnover protection during rebound.
Consistency under fatigue and repeated phases.
progressions: Remove all advance notice of scenarios.
Allow the attacking team to choose how it attempts to break the defensive system.
Change score, time and player numbers during live play.
Use uninterrupted full-match simulation.
Remove nominated defensive leaders.
Require players to review video and grade their own defensive performance.
Assess the team against a different opposition game plan in the next session.
regressions: Assess one defensive phase at a time.
Limit the defence to two available systems.
Allow brief organisation periods before restarts.
Use assistant coaches to guide separate defensive units.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor and central scoring areas.
Maintain goal-side, weak-side and behind-ball protection.
Recognise when to press, delay, match or zone.
Defend aerial, ground-level and stoppage contests.
Recover after broken lines and failed exits.
Adjust defensive risk to score and time.
Maintain legal technique and communication under fatigue.
Win possession and complete a supported transition.
Operate effectively without continuous coach direction.
matchApplication: This final assessment integrates the complete Team Defence chapter. It measures whether players can organise a full-ground defensive system, adapt it to changing match conditions, win possession and transition without sacrificing the structure required if the football turns over again.
